speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the report into Canada's newest immigrant, the former Iraqi ambassador to the U.S., raises many, many unanswered questions.
Why did the ministers of external Affairs and employment and immigration resort to finger-pointing, blaming public servants who only did their job, thereby breaking away from that long-standing parliamentary principle of ministerial responsibility?
The Clerk of the Privy Council, the Prime Minister's deputy, rejected fast-tracking Al-Mashat's case, but that recommendation was ignored. Given that no ministers were supposedly involved, who gave the order to process Al-Mashat at break-neck speed? Was the Clerk of the Privy Council interviewed by government investigators? Three government departments were involved in the case yet the ministers were never informed, and what of the unfair treatment of the thousands of potential immigrants to this country waiting years to be processed?
Yes, it is more than a coincidence. Only a full inquiry will provide Canadians with some answers.

Mr. Speaker, the throne speech this week was significant not just in the things it said, but also in things it did not say.
It did not contain even a token announcement of a national child care strategy as past speeches have. It did not contain any measures to address the tragedy of child poverty in Canada, and it did not contain any measures to get people back to work.
This government and this House made a commitment to end child poverty in Canada by the year 2000. If we are to achieve this, we must be working now to make the changes and set up a timetable for action. Unfortunately this government seems unprepared to make concrete commitments.
But the throne speech did mention a review of policies relating to the family. Tory review is a scary concept to most Canadian families and it may mean elimination of family allowances as some Conservative MPs have demanded.
This government should abandon its band-aid solutions to child poverty and start dealing with the real issues such as pay equity, an adequate minimum wage, adequate affordable housing for all Canadians, a national child care strategy, and full employment policies to get Canadians back to work.

Mr. Speaker, I know there will be little debate among Canadians about the old axiom that knowledge is power, or about the fact that education and training are crucial keys to future prosperity in Canada. Yet one of the most profound and disturbing revelations in the throne speech is that Canada has not been getting full value for the very substantial current investments being made in our search for knowledge, skill, and innovation.
I feel sure it will come as some surprise to many Canadians that the federal government alone, both directly and indirectly, is now spending close to $11 billion annually in support of education and training. These priorities are high dollar items in provincial budgets as well.

May 15, 1991
Unfortunately, however, the returns do not measure up. The high school dropout rate stands at 30 per cent and functional illiteracy among adults is equally bad, to state only two examples.
Education is a provincial responsibility in Canada but, jurisdictional sensitivities aside, there is a national interest in nurturing a new culture of learning and in developing co-operative strategies for attaining better educational results. This is a mission to which the government is committed and it is one in which all Canadians will want to join.

Mr. Speaker, since this government came to power in 1984 it has deregulated the trucking industry in Canada and implemented a free trade agreement. These two moves are systematically destroying the Canadian trucking industry.
Twelve thousand Canadian truckers lost their jobs last year. Others have been losing their trucks and their homes due to United States truckers operating in Canada, yet this government expects them to compete against United States firms whose costs that are about 25 per cent less than those in Canada. Fuel costs are less in the United States, interest rates are lower, repair costs are less, and the trucks themselves cost far less in the United States.
There is no level playing field, and yet this minister stated in the House yesterday that he is waiting for seven studies. Canadian truckers do not need studies; they need action now, government action to save their industry, their jobs and their homes.

Mr. Speaker, when Canadians think of the great national institutions which bind our country together, they think of the CBC, Air Canada and VIA Rail. They seldom, if ever, think of our political parties and their leaders. And yet a national political party and its leader must strive to find policies that will unite as many Canadians as possible by focusing on what we have in common in spite of the language, racial, regional, social and economic differences that often bitterly divide us.
The membership of a truly national party reflects as accurately as possible the demographic composition of our entire country. The compromises made by political parties, frequently considered unprincipled, are usually made in the name of the great principle of Canadian unity.
The truly national political party has been the only effective institution that we have been able to devise so far for overcoming the deep cleavages among us. It is one of Canada's greatest national inventions.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Communications remains silent while every Canadian with a telephone has a stake in the enormous corporate showdown for control of our former Crown corporation, the international telephone company, Teleglobe Canada, and its parent, Memotec Data.
To protect consumers from abuse of market power and unfair rate increases, this government in 1987 passed a law preventing Canada's large telephone companies from controlling Teleglobe.
In the interest of Canadian consumers, I ask: Does the government still oppose corporate concentration in this sector? Is the minister the anonymous "government source" who today said that Ottawa would block any changes to Memotec? How is he answering to the BCE chairman who is asking for Ottawa's permission to get his hands on Teleglobe.
While some experts say Teleglobe could fall under control this week without prior CRTC approval as is required by law, we ask: What is the minister doing to see that the letter of the law is respected and followed?
In the interest of every single Canadian who uses a telephone, where does the minister stand? What action is the minister taking to protect a fair telecommunications marketplace?

Mr. Speaker, on Sunday, May 5, a crowd of Dutch people gathered at Groesbeek Canadian War Cemetery to pay tribute to those Canadian soldiers who died so that they might be free.
May 15, 1991

The Dutch do not forget their Canadian liberators of years past. Each year they meet at one of the three Canadian war cemeteries in the Netherlands. The graves of our young Canadian soldiers are covered with flowers picked by school children.
To the Dutch it makes no difference if we come from Alberta, Quebec or Prince Edward Island, to the Dutch we are all Canadians. We are the ones who liberated their country in 1945.
At a time when Canadian unity is threatened, when Canadians are searching, we would do well to look at ourselves as others do and to count our blessings.
Canadians have much to be proud of.
speakername: Mr. Walter Van  De Walle@St. Albert

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today on the issue of the unusual procedures that were used to proclaim Bill C-79 last week.
By avoiding the normal procedures that are there for proclaiming legislation and avoiding the safeguards and the checks that are in place for that sole reason, the government has laid itself open to an accusation of abuse of power. The government's actions have left the impression that the timing of the proclamation was due to a court case or to an investigation.
I call upon the minister responsible, the government House leader, to rise in this House and list all the information from the MPs involved, their solicitors, or any other persons who acted on their behalf with any member of this cabinet.

subtopic: THE LATE HON. RICHARD BENNETT HATFIELD
THE LATE HON. RICHARD BENNETT HATFIELD
speechtext:
Although Richard Hatfield has passed from this world, Mr. Speaker, that for which he stood will never pass.
Richard Hatfield was an active participant in Canadian politics dedicated to a strong and united New Brunswick, a strong and united Canada.
He said so simply, as was his way, in an article written for New Brunswick Day:
It doesn't matter where you come from if you call New Brunswick
my placelmon foyer. We have more in common with each other than
any other peoples in the world.
He never wavered in his commitment toward that end and now that we are facing perhaps one of the greatest challenges to the future of Canada, his insight and wisdom will be sorely missed.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, Canada has lost a friend.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a delegation of three representatives of the Independent Truckers Spouses Association, led by Mrs. Janet Keusch of Alexandria, Ontario in my riding, were here today to attend a previously scheduled meeting with the Minister of Transport.
However, when time came for the meeting, the minister's staff claimed that no meeting had ever been scheduled and of course that the minister was too busy to listen to the plight of the women and children, the spouses of the truckers.
What is the Minister of Transport afraid of? Why does he refuse to meet with these women and children? I can only conclude that the minister is ashamed of his government's policies.
I call upon the minister to meet with the Independent Truckers Spouses Association immediately after Question Period. They will be waiting for him.

Mr. Speaker, in the Speech from the Throne, the federal government suggests that national unity would bring economic recovery. This is just hogwash. The facts speak for themselves. The government extolled the virtues of discipline and moderation in provincial spending. Result: Ontario's deficit tripled and reached $10 billion. While the management of the economy has to be decentralized, the government suggests centralizing it. Inflation is up in Ontario. The federal monetary policy is knocking out the provincial economies.
So far, unity has produced the following results: inconsistency and recessions. Now we should be looking for more unity. It is clear that this will only produce even more inconsistency and less economic efficiency.

May 15, 1991

Mr. Speaker, let us take a look at what the interest rates have been since 1979. The rate was 13 percent in September 1979; 12.5 percent on August 25, 1980; 22.75 percent on August 7, 1981; 16 percent on August 20, 1982; 13 percent on August 10, 1984; 10.25 percent on August 23, 1985; 9.75 percent on July 18. 1986; 10 percent on July 31, 1987; 11.25 percent on August 26, 1988; 14.25 percent on August, 1990. And now, Mr. Speaker, it is down to 9.22 percent.

Mr. Speaker, the western finance ministers have issued a report that calls for the dismantling of our national medicare program. The report demands that the federal government stop all cash payments for health and instead transfer tax points to the provinces.
The report sets out new program criteria such as affordability, efficiency, flexibility and abandons the Canada Health Act standards, public administration, comprehensiveness, universality, portability and accessibility.
Medicare is one of Canada's most treasured programs that holds this country together. I call upon the new minister of health, in the name of national unity, to state clearly that his government is committed to a national medicare program including federal funding and national standards.

Mr. Speaker, for some time this House has been treated to the featured corporate welfare bum of the month by the member for Nickel Belt.
Which NDP premier did not have the guts to tax the so-called corporate welfare bum pronounced by the member for Nickel Belt?
Whose NDP deficit is now $10 billion?
An hon. member Bob Rae.

Some hon. members Bob Rae.

Bob Rae.

Bob Rae.

Bob Rae.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is my sad duty to advise the House of the untimely death on April 23, 1991 of Michael B. Kirby, one of our table officers since 1979. A parliamentary employee for 25 years, Michael died of cancer after a short illness at the age of 51.
Most of us at one time or another have turned to Michael for procedural advice, for interpretation of the Standing Orders, or for information about precedent and practice. His counsel was always wise and thoughtful and usually given with a refreshing mix of Irish wit and charm. He was often seen standing beside the Chair offering your Speaker advice or guidance and he loved as well to recount stories.
A particular favourite of his, was the incident where a noted British Speaker was presiding over a particularly heated procedural row in the Chamber and sent a note to the clerk asking for advice. And, as Michael said it, the clerk sent a note back which said: "If I were you, Mr. Speaker, I should proceed with caution".

Mr. Kirby was a man of sound advice and it was at their own risk that Chairmen would ignore his advice. His dedication and loyalty to Parliament were unequivocal and were always evident in all the functions he performed, be it as committee clerk, head of Journals Directorate, principal clerk at the Table Research
May 15, 1991

Branch, principal clerk of the Public Bills Office or Table officer and Chair advisor.

For those of us who also have had the privilege of having Michael as a friend, his personal warmth and friendship and his unfailing generosity and good humour will be surely missed.
To his wife, Sylvie, and to his family, may I convey on behalf of all members and staff of the House of Commons my very deepest sympathy.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
The first duty of the Prime Minister is to promote the unity of Canada for the benefit of all Canadians. It is also my duty, and it should be the duty of all members of this Parliament.
How is the unity of Canada being promoted by asking Parliament to remain in the dark until September about the constitutional proposals of this government?

Mr. Speaker, no one is asking Parliament to remain in the dark. The House just came back 48 hours ago. The throne speech debate has yet to conclude. The leader of the NDP and I will be speaking this afternoon and there will be a vote tonight followed by other involvement.
There has been a recommendation from both sides of the House to proceed with care and to ensure to the extent humanly possible that the constitutional initiative is a success. The House normally would rise on June 21, return in early September, and that appears to the government, and indeed to many members of the House, to be an appropriate time to begin the formal sittings of a joint parliamentary committee.
That in no way precludes that committee from spending a very productive summer of work in anticipation of the beginning of its public hearings.
Oral Questions
Therefore I want to assure my hon. friend that while we want to make haste, we want to make haste in a prudent way to ensure the success of this constitutional initiative.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is again directed to the Prime Minister.
It is easy to start negotiations on the Constitution but very difficult to get positive results. We on this side of the House believe that there are a number of important deadlines that must be met and that time is of the essence.
Why doesn't the Prime Minister want to appoint this committee of the House of Commons and the Senate immediately, so that it can start listening to representations by Canadians, based on the specific document which will be submitted to them? They have had these papers for ages. The political will must be there to start immediately, so that by next spring, we will have a solution and will be able to meet any deadlines Quebec might have and avoid backing the country against the wall again, which would be disastrous for the future of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I find it hard to understand why my hon. friend is in such a hurry.
After Meech last summer, all members of this House asked for more intense consultations with the public. That is why we set up the Citizens Forum and the Beaudoin-Edwards Committee.
These committees will not report until July 1. This means that if we want to be consistent, we should wait until the reports on these massive consultations have been tabled before proceeding with a government initiative.
If the government were to proceed otherwise, I imagine the Leader of the Opposition would accuse me, and rightly so, of proceeding unilaterally, without waiting for the committee reports. We want to wait until the committees are ready, we will analyse their recommen-

May 15, 1991
Oral Questions
dations, and we will be ready to proceed, in the national interest, on September 1.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been asking since December that we proceed quickly in this matter. We asked that the committee not be limited only to the amending formula but that it hear the views of Canadians on a broader basis. The Prime Minister said no.
It is, in my view, extremely important to give all Canadians the opportunity to participate in a referendum where the Canadian people will be able to say "yes" to each other, and in particular to say "yes" to Quebec. Will the Prime Minister give a guarantee to this House, as he indicated to the press this morning, that he is contemplating having a referendum? Why does he not say right away that there will be a referendum on reconciliation in 1992, before the Quebec deadline?

Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend should do me the courtesy, if he is going to quote me, of quoting me accurately. In respect of a referendum this morning the transcript reveals the following: "Mulroney: I can see a referendum being helpful in a number of ways. I can see a referendum being most unhelpful if it were to divide the country and if we thought that were to be the case, we wouldn't use it".

Mr. Speaker, I would like to put a question to the Prime Minister. Yesterday the ministers of external affairs and employment and immigration in their report admitted that a memorandum had been sent by senior officials of the Department of External Affairs to the minister's office, but that no appropriate action was taken based upon that memorandum. Those ministers then took the unprecedented step of publicly identifying and blaming a senior official for that serious mistake.
I want to ask the Prime Minister: What has happened to the long-established principle of ministerial responsibility, which is the very cornerstone of our parliamentary
system? I want to ask the Prime Minister if he is prepared to release all the documents, and especially the memorandum sent to the minister, so that Canadians can know exactly what advice was tendered? I want to ask the Prime Minister if he will now show some leadership and ask the responsible ministers in this case to step aside until a proper inquiry can be had into this very serious issue?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would point out first of all that what transpired yesterday was exactly what the Minister of Employment and Immigration had said last week would be forthcoming, which was a report on what had happened.
In terms of revealing the names of officials who may have been involved in this, I would point out that it has been past practice very often to use the titles of officials who have been involved in any particular case. In this case, there were only two. From the titles that were used, that can only be one person.
Let me also say that in terms of ministerial responsibility, there is a parallel with the contempt of court case against the then Secretary of State for External Affairs and the then Minister of Employment and Immigration concerning ministerial knowledge when they did not have the information at their disposal. The court said they did not have a legal responsibility.
The cases are not totally parallel, but they are sufficiently similar, I believe, to give us a precedent.

Mr. Speaker, the issue before the House is not a question of civil liability in a court, it is the question of the accountability of ministers for their actions, their officers and their departments. That is the issue.
I want to ask the Prime Minister specifically, because this is in his own office. It is quite clear. It was admitted in the report yesterday that Mr. Paul Tellier, who is the chief public servant and who reports directly to the Prime Minister, knew about the entry of Mr. Al-Mashat several weeks before he was give final approval.
I want to ask the Prime Minister whether he was informed by Mr. Tellier. If he was not informed, why was Mr. Tellier's judgment not called into question? If the Prime Minister was informed, what did he do about it?
May 15, 1991

I want to also ask why the Secretary of State for External Affairs was not informed by memorandum when, in fact, he was clearly in Ottawa, not travelling in the Middle East, as has been reported.
In other words, the government's whole case is full of holes, omissions and a bucket full of whitewash. Surely the Prime Minister understands that if we are going to have the credibility of government at stake, he has to have a public inquiry into this case. It stinks like a sewer hole.
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend could have perhaps saved himself some degree of anxiety by reading the veiy complete report that was submitted yesterday.
He read it.

Well, he clearly did not. In regard to the specific question that he asked, indeed, Paul Tellier, on March 11, was informed that the Department of Immigration did not support the issuance of a minister's permit, nor any accelerated processing of Mr. Al-Ma-shat's application. The Clerk of the Privy Council was informed and concurred with that judgment. The Privy Council advised the Department of External Affairs that it was opposed to the issuance of this visa. Notwithstanding the firm opposition of Mr. Tellier, Mr. Al-Mashat was admitted on March 30, and we were advised on April 30. These are precisely the points that were brought forward by the ministers yesterday.
There were administrative errors made in the system for which apologies have been conveyed and accepted. It was an administrative error, no more and no less. There is no attempt to whitewash or to denigrate anyone. It was a simple administrative error that was made, acknowledged by the public servants involved and accepted by the responsible ministers.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
In the throne speech on Monday, the government stated that the economy was inextricably linked to
Oral Questions
national unity. In that throne speech, there is talk about employment and the need for a low interest rate.
In the throne speech, Canadians were promised 2.5 million new jobs by the year 2000, by the government's own projections, taking into account the growth in the labour force. This will mean that the unemployment rate in the year 2000 will still be around 10 per cent.
Is this government saying that it accepts a 10 per cent rate of unemployment and that such a rate, which now means 1.5 million unemployed, is necessary in the Conservatives' view of what constitutes competitiveness?

Mr. Speaker, the answer to that of course is no. What we are seeking to do is to reduce the number of unemployed. From 1984 until the recession hit, 1.6 million new jobs were created in Canada and Canada led the industrialized world in the creation of durable full-time jobs.
We want to replicate that in the next number of years. The process that we propose to follow is one of lower interest rates and greater investment in a non-inflationary climate. It is the only way that durable jobs can be created.
We do not accept the idea of a 10 per cent unemployment rate. In point of fact, when we formed the government in 1984, the unemployment rate in Canada was 11.7 per cent. We reduced it to 7.3 per cent, and we hope to do better in the upcoming cycle.

Mr. Speaker, despite what the Prime Minister says, the projections in their own throne speech indicated that there will still be a 10 per cent unemployment rate in the year 2000. This means more food banks, more people on welfare, and it will not mean Canadians working.
Today, Statistics Canada reports that same-day trips to the United States by Canadians are up 25 per cent. It is clear that Canadian consumers and Canadian jobs are heading south of the border. The trucking industry has reached a desperate situation. We need only go outside this House to hear what truckers are saying about their situation and the effects of this government's policies on their livelihood.

May 15, 1991
Oral Questions
Ask Canadians across this country, and they will tell you that this government's economic policies are not working. They did not want to hear more of the same in the throne speech.
Will the Prime Minister stop pursuing policies which are clearly making Canada uncompetitive and start putting in policies that will get Canadian families back to work?

Mr. Speaker, we have, of course, a great deal of sympathy for all people in Canada who are confronted with rising costs that make the sale of goods and services and products of various kinds less competitive.
My hon. friend points to the fact trips to the United States border are up dramatically. That probably has been up dramatically since the Ontario budget because with the budget in Ontario gasoline is 14.3 cents a litre, whereas in Michigan and Ohio it is 4.6 cents and 3.1 cents.

A supplementary, Mr. Speaker. The government is well aware that it is this government's policies of deregulation and the trade deal that have directly led to the state of the truckers and of the loss of jobs.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, in the Speech from the Throne the government said that economic recovery will depend on whether interest rates go down. However, according to a report published in February, at the height of the recession, the Governor of the Bank of Canada intervened directly to prevent a drop in interest rates. Could the new Minister of Finance give the House the assurance today that he personally had a meeting with the Governor of the Bank of Canada to advise him that the government's policy is to continue to lower interest rates?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, interest rates have come down by five percentage points since the high of last year, and we hope that trend will continue. That trend will continue, providing we attack the underlying causes of inflation, the inflationary
pressures, the inflationary expectations and as long as we can keep our fiscal house in order.
I can assure the hon. member that her concurrence with the Government of Ontario in chalking up a huge deficit with complete and total disregard for fiscal responsibility is not the course of action that this government wants to take. I must suggest to her that it is not the proper course for any province or any government to take in these circumstances.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. If the Al-Mashat fiasco is nothing but an administrative error, there should be no fear of an open inquiry. In the report to the immigration and external affairs ministers issued yesterday by the Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs concerning this case, we are told that the investigators interviewed "a number of the officials who had been directly involved".
My question is a simple one: Who were these officials? Which officials were not interviewed? Why were they not interviewed? Did the Clerk of the Privy Council tell the Prime Minister?

I have already indicated to my hon. friend that the Clerk of the Privy Council was advised of the possibility and he indicated his disapproval with the issuance of a visa to that individual. He conveyed that directly to the department.
Notwithstanding the firm disapproval of the Government of Canada, the visa was issued. When he arrived in Canada with the visa that ought not to have been issued, the Clerk of the Privy Council, again, and I were subsequently advised. In other words, the Clerk-
Oh, oh.

Indeed. I was advised a month after he got here. We should have been advised by the public servants in advance because Mr. Tellier, speaking for the Privy Council Office, said "do not admit him". Notwithstanding that, he was admitted. That was in violation of the procedures of the Government of Canada.
May 15, 1991

Mr. Speaker, on March 11 the director general of case management in employment and Immigration informed external affairs and the Privy Council-and we have heard this-that Mr. Al-Mashat's application should not be fast-tracked.
If he was so concerned that he called the Privy Council Office, why did he not inform his own minister, why did not those briefed immediately brief the external affairs minister, and why did Mr. Tellier not tell the Prime Minister immediately?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is missing a very key point. Of all the questions that are being asked around here on this issue, the key point is this: ministers were not informed. That was the error in judgment, not that Mr. Al-Mashat was admitted to the country, not that Mr. Al-Mashat was admitted on a fast-track. The key point was that ministers were not informed. That is the problem with this case. That is why we are saying there were errors in judgment, and that is what the report that we called for and was made public showed.

Mr. Speaker, we know that in late February the security intelligence service conducted an investigation to determine whether "Mr. Al-Mashat was a valuable source of intelligence". Mr. Reid Morden, the director of the security intelligence service, was aware of it. Will the government not admit that the director of the security intelligence service, Mr. Reid Morden, informed the former Solicitor General prior to Mr. Al-Mashat arriving in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is a committee which meets to discuss matters such as my hon. friend refers to. The membership of the committee changes from time to time. Whoever is familiar with that particular file sits on the committee. All the proper procedures were taken.

Mr. Speaker, this sc-called comprehensive report that the government issued yesterday was strangely silent when it came to the role of the former Solicitor General and the role of the director of the security intelligence service. I put the question to the present Solicitor General: Exactly what was the role of Mr. Reid Morden, the director of
Oral Questions
the security intelligence service, and when did he inform the former Solicitor General?

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the role of the director of the security intelligence service and CSIS in these matters is to examine the situation and determine whether or not the individual involved is of any use to Canada in terms of intelligence matters.

Mr. Speaker, I want to come back to the Solicitor General.
In view of the concern of Canadians about the extent to which procedures were violated, and the extent to which a gentleman whose record is documented in a report which I received this morning written by him which includes, among other things, the statement that members of Amnesty International are bigots who make a noise and: "I would like to see one victim of chemical weapons inside Iraq".
In view of that kind of documented background, I want to ask the Solicitor General once again if he will clarify at what point was his predecessor as Solicitor General informed by CSIS that Al-Mashat was seeking to enter Canada? Was that before the visa was issued or afterwards? When was it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is my information that the previous Solicitor General was informed after Mr. Al-Mashat entered Canada.

supplementary, Mr. Speaker, for the Prime Minister.
I want to ask the Prime Minister first of all, why is it that the director of CSIS did not inform the Solicitor General about this very serious matter?
Second, if the Prime Minister is not concerned that the former Minister of Employment and Immigration, who found out about this matter on April 16, did not do any follow-up inquiry whatsoever other than issuing what she called a sharp note after being scraped off the ceiling, and did not even bother telling the next minister of immigration that this was a problem, does the Prime Minister not recognize that Canadians do not accept this explanation? They do not accept civil servants being blamed, and they do not accept this cover-up of ministerial responsibility.

May 15, 1991
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member would look at the report which he has in hand, he will first of all see the dates on which CSIS made a routine report to officials and thought that was the end of it.
If the hon. member is suggesting that a sharp note to a department is not sufficient, let me just point out to the hon. member that also in this report it indicates that there was follow-up.
My department and the people who work for me have always recognized that if I send a note, I expect some follow-up. There was in this case.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
The trucking industry in our country is taking a brutal beating since the government introduced deregulation, thereby putting our Canadian truckers on an unequal and impossible footing in comparison to their American counterparts.
Since the Prime Minister has spoken so proudly in the past of having been a truck driver himself, when will the government stop hiding behind the studies? Will the Prime Minister request the Minister of Transport to at least have the decency of meeting with truckers. Together we can hammer out real and immediate solutions so that Canadian truckers can once again begin to earn a living, just like the Prime Minister did a few years ago?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell the hon. member that it is precisely to take away from the discussion the type of things he says are not exact.
For instance, he says that the effects of the government deregulation has had a very negative impact on some aspects of the trucking industry. He forgets to say that the federal fuel excise tax in Canada is one-third less than in the U.S.
He also forgets to mention that the removal of the manufacturers' sales tax has reduced the tax on fuel by 2.5 cents per litre. He also forgets to mention that the recent decision of the Ontario government to increase the tax on fuels by 2 cents a litre immediately and
another 2 cents in January is also increasing the problem of the trucking industry.
We did not decide to begin the studies and analyses just for the fun of it. It was understood by all stakeholders in the trucking industry; the provinces, the Canadian Trucking Association, the unionized truckers, the Coalition of Independent Owner-Operators and federal departments, that we would form a task force to examine all aspects of the trucking industry in Canada. That task force decided to have seven studies. They are not frivolous studies. Some of the studies are on the effect of taxation on Canada-U.S. competitiveness, assessment of Canada-U.S. trucking cabotage, comparison of Canada and U.S. trucking costs in transborder-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. minister can find another way to provide that information. The hon. member for York West.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the same minister. It has become painfully obvious that this minister does not understand, or appreciate, the absolute terrible state facing Canadian truckers and their families across the country.
How can the minister and this government expect the trucking industry to survive when Canadian truckers in increasing numbers have lost their rigs, their earnings, their profits, their homes and their dignity to the unfettered American competition? Does he not think it is time that he came out from behind these studies and studied the problems facing real Canadians, that he sit down and get some real solutions so that together our industry may have a chance of not only competing but of surviving?

Mr. Speaker, contrary to the customary way of doing things by members on the other side, we believe in the notion that before we can arrive at solutions we must identify the real problems. This is what all the stakeholders have decided to do, not just the government itself. They have agreed that before we can discuss things intelligently, we must have the facts.
We have met with the Coalition of Independent Owner-Operators group that represents 7,000 members. I have met with representatives of the Canadian Trucking Association. I have been open to discussions with all authorized representatives of the trucking industry. We sympathize very much with the truckers. We are trying to find a complete and permanent solution rather than to
May 15, 1991

Oral Questions
try to have temporary solutions, which is the favourite subject of members on the other side.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the same minister. Already in my riding of Haldimand-Norfolk three trucking firms have collapsed under the weight of this government's policies.
The minister fails to realize that bankers will not wait until he finishes wall-papering his office with studies. Truckers are losing their jobs. They are losing their trucks and they are losing their homes. It is completely in the power of this House to do something about it. What is the minister waiting for?

Mr. Speaker, I believe that the member was not listening when I gave the previous answer. This matter was the subject of very serious discussions among all the parties involved last June. At that time we established a process of having seven studies that will establish a level playing field. These studies are in preparation and will be given to the task force shortly. At that time we will know exactly what are the complete problems, the hypothetical solutions and we will take that report very seriously.

Mr. Speaker, I was listening to the minister. The minister said that no action would be taken by the government until all the studies were complete. I have a letter from the former Minister of Transport and it says in it: "I have no intention however of waiting until all the studies are completed to take action".
Will the minister now honour the words of his predecessor and take action today to help these Canadian truckers?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should know that one of the main actions we took to improve the lot of the trucking industry was to remove the manufacturers' sales tax of 13.5 per cent. But we could only do it after a year and a half of bickering by the Liberal Party and their friends in the Senate.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of the Environment. An environmental disaster has been discovered in Mercier, Quebec. It is clear that Laidlaw-Tricil broke the law. It is clear that this company is an environmental criminal and that the contamination at the Mercier site is only the tip of the iceberg. Will the minister apply the sanctions provided under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act? Will the government act now?
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member, I was informed that containers had been discovered on a site, a lot in Mercier. The hon. member is probably aware that a memorandum of understanding between the federal and provincial governments provides for clean-ups of unsupervised sites. Now it seems that this particular site, as the hon. member implied in his question, belongs to a company known as Laidlaw which has started clean-up procedures. I may remind the hon. member that under Quebec law, the company may be charged. Meanwhile, we will let the investigation proceed and testing continue, and subsequently, Mr. Speaker, we will take appropriate action, if necessary.

Mr. Speaker, Quebec is sick and tired of being exploited by environmental criminals who unlawfully use the provinces as a dump for dangerous products. My question is directed to the Solicitor General. We have already seen Quebec used as a dump for toxic and dangerous products. We saw it in Saint-Jean, we saw it in Saint-Basile and we see it again today in Mercier. Is the minister prepared to order the RCMP to conduct an investigation of course, with the co-operation of the Surete du Quebec to examine the whole issue of transportation inside and outside Quebec under the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can assure you and the members of this House that we share the concern of opposition members and the hon. member who just spoke about the transportation of toxic wastes of any kind. However, I may remind the hon. member that it is also important to avoid making general and sometimes unfounded allega-

May 15, 1991
Oral Questions
tions, and that the truth and the facts must be respected. Actually, since I became a member of this government, I have been impressed by the fact that there has been very little political partisanship on environmental issues. There is a tendency to avoid such tactics.
Mr. Speaker, I want to make it clear that as far as I know, governments have never taken lightly situations involving the transportation of toxic waste, and that when violations were discovered, they were thoroughly investigated. That is what is happening today in the case of the Mercier site, which was mentioned yesterday on the news and in the media. My department intends monitor the situation very closely, as has always has been its policy in the past, and we will also continue to monitor any similar allegations.

Mr. Speaker, the minister of immigration knew about the Al-Mashat matter on April 12; indeed, she reprimanded her department on April 16, but her colleague, the minister of external affairs says he did not know until May 7.
My question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. Could he tell us today why the minister of immigration did not tell of this matter to the minister of external affairs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the then minister of immigration found out on April 16. The memo was dated April 12 and reached the then minister on April 16. A note was sent back to the department saying that this was not to happen again and looking for follow up. At that point there was no particular reason to inform another minister because there was no way of knowing where the error had taken place.
But what is clearly important is that action was called for on that date, but the report was not made before the transfer of responsibilities to another minister.

Mr. Speaker, I know it is astounding to the Canadian people that there was no
reason to tell the then minister of external affairs about an ambassador from a country with whom we had been at war a scant two weeks before. More important, the minister learned, as she says now, of the Al-Mashat matter on April 16 and allegedly hit the roof. But no investigation began into this matter until May 8, the day after the press broke the story. Inquiring minds would like to know what was the hold up.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, inquiring minds normally take advantage of the material that is put in front of them. As the hon. member will see in the report, there was follow up within the Department of Immigration and that there is, indeed, a note in the Case Management Branch on May 1.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
The government has attempted to convince parliamentarians and, through Parliament, Canadians that no minister had any idea whatsoever about the arrival in Canada and request for asylum by Mr. Al-Mashat. That is what the government has claimed.
The government made clear in its report published very recently on this whole affair that a memorandum was sent to the office of the former Secretary of State for External Affairs on March 8. This memorandum requested that the minister be informed of the request by Al-Mashat for residency in Canada.
The minister said in her public statement yesterday: "The one memorandum sent to the minister's office via the senior departmental assistant prior to the arrival did not clearly seek ministerial view or concurrence". We are being told that because the memo was less than crystal clear the ministers are absolved.
Will the Deputy Prime Minister table that memo and make it public? Let Parliament judge whether or not ministers were informed of this matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as usual we are getting very mixed signals from people in the opposition. On the one hand they say that names should not have been
May 15, 1991

Privilege
released and now they are asking for more names. I do not understand what they want. They do not like the names we released, they want other names. Maybe that is what the difficulty is.
The point is that what is laid out in here was a report to deputy ministers by two neutral people within the Public Service who entered into this issue very carefully. My successor, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, had said a report would be made. A report was made. It is as complete as it can be and it tells people what they need to know.
The critical point which the hon. member continues to miss is that ministers were not told. That was the error, that was what was wrong and that is why ministers themselves were not pleased.

Mr. Speaker, what we are looking for is not names, we are looking for the truth.
The fact of the matter is that the senior political staff in the office of the minister of external affairs were informed. A memo was sent. The senior public servant, who reports directly to the Prime Minister, Mr. Tellier, was informed. It is incredible that when the ambassador to a country with whom we were at war seeks asylum in Canada, no minister claims to know about it. We simply do not believe it. Canadians do not believe it. Make the memo public and let us judge for ourselves. Put an end to this whitewash and this hanging of innocent public servants.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the report speaks for itself. The report goes into some considerable detail in a very precise form as to what happened during the process of this incident.
I may say as well that in a different case where the two ministers did know in advance that someone was seeking to come to Canada, that was turned down. Therefore, that should have set the stage for any future people who chose to come to Canada under similar circumstances. I do not know what else ministers can be expected to do.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport.
Between January 1,1989 and February 10,1990, 81 out of the 174 routes serving Abitibi were eliminated, 69 of them for lack of available crews or trains.
My question is this: Can the minister tell us today why the president and the management of VIA Rail have deliberately cut passenger service in Abitibi on several occasions to the detriment of both patrons and employees of VIA Rail?

Mr. Speaker, I want to praise again the hon. member for Abitibi for his unrelenting concern for his area and all that affects it.
I also want to tell him, as he probably knows already, that VIA Rail is a Crown corporation with its own administrative structure. I can confirm, however, that the Abitibi line is under examination by VIA Rail because of the infrastructure problems it has experienced in recent months. We are still monitoring the situation through, as I said, the administrative structure of the corporation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a point of personal privilege

May 15, 1991
Routine Proceedings
arising from a response to a question on the Order Paper, pursuant to Standing Order 48(2). I provided notice to the Chair on April 15 of this year.
This is the earliest possible opportunity for me to raise this point of personal privilege.
On April 11 last, I placed a question on the Order Paper for the Minister of State for Multiculturalism and Citizenship. The question dealt with the involvement of a Dr. Ralph Agard and the establishment of a race relations network. This question was subdivided into eight questions.
I believe that my personal privilege as a member of this House was violated because of a response provided by the minister. My question asked whether Dr. Agard had received any contracts, either directly or indirectly, since April 1, 1985, other than for a feasibility study for the network. The minister's response was "No."
It has been brought to my attention that this response was incorrect and that the minister was probably aware of this fact at the time he answered my questions.
On June 9, 1989, the minister announced three race relations initiatives. The second, according to the press release from the minister's office, was the commissioning of International Briefing Associates to develop a national action plan to propose specific concrete measures that would lead to improved police-minority relations.
I provided the Chair with a copy of this press release. I have also provided a copy of a discussion paper summarizing the consultations carried out by this organization. It is clear from this document that Dr. Agard benefited directly from a contract with the Ministry of State for Multiculturalism and Citizenship. This is in direct contradiction to the response of the question that I placed on the Order Paper.
How am I to perform my duties as a member of this Parliament if the responses ministers of the Crown provide to questions are inaccurate? Had the minister taken the time since he provided the response to correct this error, I would not have risen on this point of privilege. He has not done so.
Mr. Speaker, I urge you to assist me in finding a means to remedy this situation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ORDER PAPER QUESTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is fairly obvious to the House and to the Chair that this is not a case of privilege. As the Chair is well aware, there is never a case of privilege when there is a matter of dispute over an answer.
The Speaker is also aware that to any question raised in the House or put on the Order Paper I could rise on behalf of the minister in my capacity as Parliamentary Secretary to the Government House Leader and say: "Yes, no, maybe". The truth is that it is an answer and it is not, therefore, a subject of privilege here in this House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, I would ask that you rule quickly on this one so that we can get on with the business before us.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member has raised an issue which is not an unusual kind of issue to raise. The hon. member is not satisfied with the response given. The difficulty that is always with the Chair in these cases is that there are often very great differences of interpretation on answers that are given. In this case, I think the hon. parliamentary secretary is correct. It is not a question of privilege, it is a question of disagreement over certain facts and answers that were given. The hon. member may, perhaps, have another means to pursue the matter.
I thank the hon. member for giving me notice and complete detail of her question of privilege.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I interrupted my remarks yesterday I was presenting some of my views, the views of a number of my constituents and the views of women across this country on the crucial matter of violence against women and its escalation in Canada today.
There are questions the women of Canada are asking, which have arisen due to the Speech from the Throne. They would like to hear from, and are hoping they will hear very soon, the right hon. Prime Minister. We heard in the Speech from the Throne that a blue ribbon panel of Canadian men and women will be appointed to deal
with the question of violence against women. This, as I said, raises a number of concerns.
As I said yesterday, I and several other members of this House have been, since November, members of a subcommittee on the status of women dealing with the question of violence against women. We have heard many eloquent witnesses over the past several months and have more witnesses scheduled to appear in the next few months.
Many of us, many women's groups across this country-such as the YWCA of Canada, the National Action Committee, the Canadian Research Institute for the Advancement of Women, and a number of others-have called for a royal commission on violence against women.
The major reasons we have called for this royal commission is that, first of all, the research into violence against women and its causes still tends to be, in this country and in other countries of the west, anecdotal as opposed to empirical. We also believe that a royal commission, properly constituted, would shine the light of publicity and provide this frightening and rapidly growing problem the kind of notice and the kind of credibility it requires in all comers of this country. The sad fact is that too many people in Canada still believe that incidents of violence against women do not happen to people in the so-called mainstream, that they happen to some mythical underclass who really are the architects of their own destruction.
The women of Canada are concerned and many supportive men in Canada are concerned that this issue not be shuffled off. We want to know what a blue ribbon panel is. More than that, we want to have a royal commission. We want to seek and find and publish the answers as to what the root causes are to the questions of violence against women.
We know, for example, that alcohol plays a part. We know that the cycle of violence from childhood plays a part. We know that economic problems play a part. However, none of these things is necessarily common to every incident. What we need is a royal commission rooted in the experience of women and some men who work in the front lines, in transition houses, in shelters, and in women's centres across this country. We need to hear from police officers, we need to hear from judges, and we need to hear most especially from the women who deal in the transition houses on a daily basis with the battered and injured women who are the victims every
May 15, 1991

day and every night in Canada of an horrendous wave of violence.
I call upon the Prime Minister and the government to let us know what their plans are. I beg them in the name of the women of Canada, indeed in the name of all of those who believe in a truly just nation, to deal with this problem as soon as possible and to deal with it in the way that the women of Canada and those experts in the field have asked.
I call upon the Prime Minister to appoint a royal commission into violence against women.

The fear of some women is that the matter could be shunted aside into a royal commission, that it could be put on the back burner, so to speak. If they send it to a royal commission, they can forget about it.
This is not the kind of royal commission that women's groups, we on the opposition side of the House, and we
The Address
on the subcommittee on violence against women have been talking about. We are talking about a royal commission that is rooted in women's experience. That is the phrase that has been used by proponents of this commission over and over again. We need women who have spent time and gained expertise in this area, and we have them right across the country in every province, in every region: north, south, east, west. They are there and they are willing to serve.

By the way, the amount of money the government has allotted for second-stage housing would build one small apartment building in each province in Canada. The problem is we need first-stage housing and first-stage assistance. For every 10 women who seek assistance, five are turned away.

Mr. Speaker, I would like first to offer my congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, the member for Saint-Maurice and the member for Regina-Wascana. I have absolutely no doubt that their words will persuade all
members, unanimously, to adopt the Speech from the Throne.

Mr. Speaker, in the history of nations as in the life of individuals, there are times when it behooves us to consider the hopes we all have for the future on the basis of past history.
Canada, as a country, and all of us as Canadian citizens have reached one of those crucial moments when we have to draw from our historical background the resolve and confidence we need to face our destiny. In coming to terms with our identity, we must now decide what we want to become.
This session of Parliament is sure to go down in the history of the Canadian Federation.

We have great problems to confront, and it will help if we can maintain a sense of historical perspective. In the debates leading up to Confederation, the public finances of Canada were in bad shape; the economic outlook was uncertain as Britain declared for free trade as opposed to Imperial preference; Lower Canada felt, even then, that its language and culture would be swamped by Upper Canada; and later, Mr. Speaker, there were even separatists elected to the House of Commons-from Nova Scotia.
Some years later, Laurier spoke of his fears for Canada. He said:
The Province of Manitoba is in open revolt-the Province of Nova
Scotia demands its separation from Confederation-In fact-from
East to West and from North to South-the prevailing feeling in
Canada is one of unrest and uneasiness, of discontent and irritation.
Three years later, in 1890, Laurier had occasion to warn that:
We have come to a period in a history of this young country when
premature dissolution seems to be at hand.
But leaders persisted, and Canadians prevailed. [Translation]
Like our predecessors, because of the trust placed in us by our fellow citizens, each of us has the historical responsibility to help strenghten the bonds that hold this great country together.
May 15, 1991

In this House, as members from all political parties, we represent the various regions of the country. We each have our political affiliation and our own views on how to solve the country's problems. However, if we are to succeed, we must never forget that what bonds us is stronger and more precious than any divisive factors that might break us up as a people.
Indeed, the leader of the opposition was right when he said recently that the future of Canada is more important than a political career. At the beginning of this new session, I want to reaffirm that both myself and my party fully intend to work with all members whatever their party who share the desire and the will to build a stronger Canada while, at the same time, respecting the legitimate aspirations of the regions and the provinces.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, now is the time to move beyond special interests. Now is the time to speak for the national interest. That is the role and the responsibility of the Parliament of Canada. There is no greater constituent assembly than the House of Commons and this House of Commons will assume national leadership.
Our constituents have sent us here to debate the issues and to resolve Canada's problems. The problems are serious. But so are the opportunities. Men and women of good will, of vision, who believe in Canada, who know of the magnificence of our own citizenship and our own heritage, will confront this challenge. We will prevail because Canada's interests, the national interests, demands it and Canadians will ensure that that turns out to be the case.
We all have partisan interests and instincts. That is the nature of politics. I occasionally, not often, indulge in partisan comments myself.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No, never.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
But on this issue, Mr. Speaker, we are all partisans, partisans of Canada.
I have said it before, and I tell this House now, what matters is not the next election, what matters is Canada; only Canada.
The Address
While leadership is required, there is also a time to listen. And we are now listening carefully to what Canadians from every comer of the country have to tell us, their representatives. After the consultation, precise and perhaps far-reaching initiatives will be announced. When that time comes, we will do so with the certainly that the Canadian population has had the opportunity to offer us their opinions and the chance to express their own hopes and dreams and those of their children for the future.
Make no mistake, the government and the Parliament of Canada, all parliamentarians, will play a leadership role in this debate, not simply as arbiters, but as proponents and strong defenders of the national interest.
I noted the comment of one of the members of the Citizens' Forum who said Canadians were ready for a new Charlottetown. Our challenge in the government and Parliament of Canada is to provide a focus for these voices which seek change. I am confident that Canada and Canadians will rise to that challenge.
We are called upon now to find a common vision and a common purpose. Perhaps it is not as complicated as some may believe. Irrespective of where we sit in this House, irrespective of our own personal backgrounds; if we bear in mind our common values of compromise, tolerance and respect for one another's language and religion, culture and region, we will come through this challenging time in the life of our country and Canada will be a better and a stronger nation for it.
We will need all of those values if we are to define a new vision of this country. We are challenged to bring forth not just a vision that Canadians will accept, but one they want.

Those who signed the British North America Act were not dreamers or sorcerers' apprentices. They had a realistic and pragmatic concept of the geographic, cultural, social and economic factors that would determine our future on this continent.

The Canadian economic union succeeded for a very simple reason. It went hand in hand with a Canadian political union. In our history books we focus on Confederation as an act of accommodation and indeed, it was

May 15, 1991
The Address
that. We tend to overlook that it was an act of separation as well, an act of separation from the 1840 Union and that too is an important consideration.
In choosing federalism over a unitary system, we put an end to the notion that the path to Canadian unity lay through submerging our diversity in a unitary state. Rather, we chose a system in which provinces are sovereign in their respective areas, but Canadians are associated on matters we have in common.
Our economic and political union, founded on generous ideals and on sound principles, has proved remarkably adaptable in the 20th century. It facilitated the entry and the development of six "new" provinces into the Canadian family. It has evolved in response to depression and war, the growth of the modem welfare state, massive immigration and the post-war baby boom. In the face of the stresses and strains of the past decades, Canada has developed innovative and sophisticated solutions to meet remarkable new challenges.
Today Canada is one of the world's leading economic powers. Our standard of living has consistently been among the highest in the entire industrialized world.
Our record of growth in job creation has been one of the best among the industrialized, G-7, and OECD nations in the last six years. The strength of our economy and our solidarity have allowed us to implement cultural and social programs that express our generosity, our values and, in many ways, are regarded with envy and admiration by most people around the world.
We are one of the great trading nations of the world and a strong voice for international co-operation. We have earned our place at the G-7 table. We have earned our place at G-7 and we are going to keep it.

Some self-styled economists say otherwise, but the Canadian economic union has served Quebec well since Confederation. In fact, it is rather ironic to hear these people urging Quebecers to leave a federation that, according to them, can only spell economic disaster, and then turn around and say there must be an economic union with Canada.
Mr. Speaker, although they refuse to consider being involved in developing Canada's financial policies, they do want a monetary union with Canada. The Allaire and Belanger-Campeau reports acknowledged that Quebec would be well advised to maintain this union. However, these reports, some of which were not necessarily prepared by the Commission but by certain groups working for the Commission, are on the wrong track when they maintain that economic ties will not necessarily be affected by political separation.
Quebec is an integral part of the Canadian economic union. It is a vast market for other parts of the country and, in turn, enjoys extraordinary benefits as a result of its participation in the economies of the other provinces. In fact, six of our provinces, including Quebec, sell more manufactured goods to other provinces than to foreign countries. It would be unrealistic to think that an economic union could be run effectively in the next century without the central government playing a major role.
Mr. Speaker, why would Canadians jeopardize an economic union that has worked so well and that still has so much to offer? No one claims that Canada is perfect, but we are all aware of the benefits we have enjoyed in this country for almost 125 years. The most eloquent example of economic and political integration today comes to us from Europe, especially from France and England, the mother countries of Canada's two great linguistic families.
All over the European continent, we see nations that have waged bloody wars practically from generation to generation during the last millennium and who, thirty years ago, started to create an open and dynamic economic union of over 300 million people.
Mr. Speaker, how can anyone seriously consider strengthening an economic union that is so vital and necessary to the future of Quebecers and Canadians, while at the same time isolating the members of that union? Quebecers know Canada isn't perfect, Mr. Speaker, but as a Quebecer-and I said as much recently in my own riding of Charlevoix-I know the people of my native province are deeply attached to Canada and that they are very proud of its great achievements.

The Address
Mr. Speaker, in spite of certain speeches and impressions, Quebecers have no intention whatsoever to tear their Canadian passeport and plunge into the unknown. That, I can guarantee you, Mr. Speaker.
A month ago, Mr. Jacques Delors, chairman of the European Economic Community, during an official visit in Ottawa, was asked a few questions on national unity. I did not provoke the question. It was a spontaneous question asked by a distinguished member of the public gallery. The answer given by Mr. Delors, a former minister of Economy in the French government, when asked about Canadian unity, could not be clearer; here is what he said here in Ottawa a few steps away from here:
As you know, in Europe, we are working on a certain political union, a federal state. Our conception is federal, he went on to say, and it provides for a common policy on external and economic affairs, a common currency, a common central bank, and an economic policy parallel to this monetary policy, both policies being strongly convergent.
And he concluded:
So, in Europe we are uniting because we believe that nowadays we do not have individually a sufficient liberty of movement to guarantee our autonomy, our well-being and reach our goods.
Certain people in Quebec would want us to believe that, while prosperity in Europe will be gained through unity, our prosperity in Canada and Quebec can gain through disunity. What an illogic and unacceptable statement that is for Canadians and Quebecers!
I am sure that the best way to protect the French language, to guarantee that it will continue to express the characteristic spirit of the French majority in Quebec and of the French minorities outside Quebec, is to maintain the stability of our political institutions and the economic prosperity which derives from it. That is because Canada, unlike many countries, respects diversity, one of it's fundamental principles. The influence of the French language will extend over large areas only if it is used in great alliances and the main international forums.
Mr. Speaker, I believe it is quite true to say that the few French immigrants who settled here three centuries and a half ago would marvel at the sight of Canada today, the world's second largest francophone country and, with France, on of the main supporters of the international francophonie.
[English}
The great preoccupation of Quebec and French Canada is now, as it has been for many decades, the preservation of cultural and linguistic heritage. Let us not forget that this undertaking was given in the most solemn way in 1867.
There are political groups in Canada who now tell their supporters that this country should plan to get along without Quebec or that Quebec can and should get along without Canada.
These groups, at opposite ends of the disunity spectrum, stand for fragmentation whereas Canadians and Quebecers have always stood for solidarity, unity and strength. The greatest assurance this House and this country can give French Canada of the respect of its language and its culture is the assurance that that language will be respected and honoured in the rest of Canada now and as we work and live together in a greater and greater way across the nation in our homes and in our lives.

speechtext:
Quebec wants the tools necessary to protect and affirm its distinctiveness. Last June 23,1 said that before we tried again to amend the Constitution, we would have to clear up some of the difficulties and misunderstandings and find a better way to amend the Constitution. So we set up a citizens forum to listen to and gather the views of as many Canadians as possible in as short a time as possible.
I think, under very difficult circumstances, the citizens forum has done a remarkable job. I have every confidence that its final report will be a valuable contribution to the proposals the government will bring forward in the autumn.
Running on a parallel track is the Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, known as the Beaudoin-Edwards Committee, which is seeking the views of Canadians on improving the way we change our Constitution. The excellence of its work has been commented on in editorials across the country.
On behalf of all members of the House I want to pay tribute to members of that committee, who have done such outstanding work.

May 15, 1991
The Address
Clearly, we must find a better way to transact constitutional affairs in this country. I am hopeful that the joint committee will help point us all in a better direction.
The reports of both the citizens forum and the joint committee are due by July 1, and the government will give every consideration to their recommendations in formulating its proposals over the summer months. Then, in a little more than three months, the government will submit its proposals to the new joint Parliamentary Committee on Constitutional Affairs. The committee will travel the country for several months, seeking the views of Canadians in every comer of this land.
The committee, as noted in the Speech from the Throne, will meet legislators from parallel committees of commissions in other provinces; perhaps on the floors of their own legislatures. It will also meet with aboriginal groups across the country.
This is an inclusive process open to all Canadians. I see nothing exclusionary about it.
I give this House an undertaking, on behalf of the government, that the government will be very open-minded to constructive amendments offered in the spirit of improving its proposals and broadening the consensus that Canadian unity needs and demands.
Reform of the Senate of Canada and of other institutions will improve and ensure both greater fairness and greater responsiveness. Oftentimes we are told that in some cities in western Canada people live some 2,000 miles from Ottawa and yet they feel that they are 2 million miles away because of the manner in which some concerns are dealt with. A lot of that has to do with the deficiencies in some of our institutions and the lack of responsiveness to the calls of the regions. Reform of the Senate and of other institutions to ensure both fairness and responsiveness means a great deal in western Canada and in many areas of Atlantic Canada.
People in Ontario are concerned about the growing costs of government generally and about the need to compete with our world-wide trading partners.
Aboriginal Canadians continue their quest for social justice and constitutional assurances.
This round will be a Canadian round, east and west, north and south, English and French speaking. All Canadians can and will benefit from constitutional reform.

speechtext: Hear, hear.
