speechtext:
While there is no doubt that we are living through a crisis in the life of this country, it can also be viewed as an opportunity. It is an opportunity to do even better. The only deadline we face is the time needed to build a consensus among Canadians on how to improve Canada. Our only challenge is to recognize that a strong, economic and political union is fundamental to our collective prosperity.
Today I want to address, very briefly, some of the economic issues and options that will underlie the government's proposals. Others have referred to them. No one is re-inventing the wheel, as the Leader of the Opposition or the Leader of the NDP has pointed out in different circumstances. The Constitution clearly must guarantee the free flow of people and goods and services, capital and technology within the federation. It must also provide a broad framework for the economic union and establish key economic rights. The need for competitiveness and the imperatives of economic success make it essential that the provincial governments work with the federal government.
We must ask ourselves some basic and blunt questions about the efficiency of our economic union. Is it normal, for example, that internal barriers make Canada a much more balkanized domestic market than Europe or the United States, geographic groupings with 10,12, 13 times the population of this country? Why is it easier for some firms to do business overseas than in a neighbouring province? Should Canadian firms be handicapped by the need to comply with two sales tax schemes; one federal and one provincial? I know some people will argue that we should not have any at all. I see my friend from the NDP applauding, but I can tell him one little fact of life: if you want sound and magnificent social services, we have got to pay for them.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I say that with respect to my friend from Regina.

Do we really need three separate security regulators when all over the world countries are moving to a much more centralized regulatory regime? Does it make any sense that a trust company conceivably can face 11 separate sets of rules and regulations if that corporation wishes to operate across Canada when the goal in Europe is to allow institutions in one country to operate under a single licence right across the community? Is the population well served when a provincial government raises its deficit dramatically while the federal government and all other provincial governments seek to reduce the financial burden of the nation?
Sovereignty is the capacity to develop fundamental common values along with the economic strength to sustain and defend them. A country whose public finances drift into disrepair creates problems not only for future generations but for its capacity to act independently and assertively on the world scene. In the conduct of its public finances, Canada has been flirting with danger. Since 1984 we have made some progress in regaining control of the public finances. The rate of growth of program spending in Ottawa since 1984 has increased 3.7 per cent per year below the rate of inflation. In the previous 15 years the annual rate of increase of program spending on average was 13.9 per cent per year every year for 15 years.
There are consequences for overspending. There are consequences for everything we do. I mention this simply to make the point that at the end of the day this nation needs the resources if we are going to remain strong and united. A national debt of roughly $18 billion in 1969 with no deficit was transformed by 1984 into a national debt of $206 billion and an annual deficit of $38.9 billion.
My hon. friend from Newfoundland asks a very good question: What is it now? He is quite right, it was $206 billion and it is now $389 billion, but I want to point out to him that almost all of the increase in the national debt since 1984 is the result of compound interest on the glut that we have had. My hon. friend will understand that, believe it or not, this is not said with the view to scoring a given point. It is to try and make a point. I know that he would make the point if he were on this side, pointing out the gravity of the same problem.
The Address
The problem is that when we began, 12 cents of every tax dollar was going to service the debt. With this size of debt, 32 cents of every dollar was required to pay the interest on the debt. So financing the deficit sucks up huge amounts of capital that are no longer available for education and for health care, defence expenditures, foreign aid, and assistance to building a better quality of life for Canadians.
This Constitution and national unity cannot be discussed in abstract terms. There are some very hard realities that we have to consider. If all of that amount, 32 cents, 33 cents, 34 cents per dollar, the second worst record in the industrialized world, if that amount is going to bond holders, to people holding our debt, that means we have the $20 billion and $30 billion per year going out, which in comparative terms is not going out of other treasuries, that we do not have for investments in infrastructure, for investments in social programs, for investments that strengthen the unity of the nation.
I think it is important to point out because without economic strength, and if you add to the deficit and you continue to add to your debt service costs, then what is left to provide programs for Canadians? How would we fund medical and pension benefits for an aging population? How would we invest in infrastructure improvements? How would we honour our obligations in the world?
I do not think it is a partisan statement to say that to believe in sound finances for the Government of Canada does not signal a lack of compassion. It signals-and I think I can say that on behalf of all members-a sense of realism that, without fiscal discipline and sound economic growth, the only thing that governments can deliver is a fool's paradise and that is not good enough for Canadians.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
The questions of our unity and prosperity cannot be considered apart. When Canadians are troubled over their future together, it sends very negative signals to the investment community. When our prosperity is diminished, it weakens the foundations of our living together. The unity of Canada is tied to our competitive position in the world and our competitiveness is a pillar of Canadian unity.

May 15, 1991
The Address

The Speech from the Throne mentioned the major problems facing us and the decisions we must make. As we predicted, there are now signs that we are coming out of the recession. Last month, the unemployment rate fell for the first time since last June. The increase in jobs during the past two months was also a positive sign. In April, housing starts increased by nearly 30 per cent over previous months. Confidence in the business community is now at its highest level in seven years. Interest rates, the cornerstone of all genuine and durable economic recovery, dropped 5 per cent over the past year and have gone down 1 per cent since the federal Budget.
However, we cannot, in the long term, continue to take our prosperity for granted. We cannot afford to sit back and rely only on Canada's vast natural resources. A difficult road lies ahead if we are to raise our productivity to the same level as that of our competitors. However, instead of letting ourselves be paralysed by our problems, I say we should take advantage of this opportunity to strengthen Canada.
We must consider how to increase our productivity which alone can create durable prosperity. Government deficits and letting the Bank of Canada print more and more bills leads to inflation. It may get us a few part-time jobs but it does not produce any durable wealth. Productivity alone is the key to a great nation's durable prosperity. Clearly, we have not been able to maximize the principal agent of our prosperity our human resources.
In the Speech from the Throne, it was announced that we would initiate a debate on education, while fully observing the jurisdiction of the provinces in this field, and that we would do so by publishing a discussion paper on learning. Together, as citizens and parents, we must stop the draining away of our young talent and help them stay in school instead of dropping out, now that education, excellence and training are vital to success on the labour market.

The Speech from the Throne set out the problem quite clearly. The issue in this regard is not exclusively or even primarily money. Canada already spends more
money per capita on education than almost any other industrialized country in the world. I believe the exception is Sweden.
From the federal level alone, the federal government spends almost $11 billion directly and indirectly on education and training, to say nothing of the billions that are spent by the appropriate provincial governments in providing facilities and training for our young people.
Yet, the issue remains: results. Three out of 10 students drop out of high school before graduating. In some jurisdictions, it is higher, it approaches four out of 10. Four out of 10 adults cannot read or do mathematics well enough to perform everyday tasks.
Canadian industry spends less than half as much on training its employees as American industry does, a fifth as much as the Japanese, and an eighth as much as the Germans. This is not the kind of performance that will guarantee increasing prosperity for our children.
In fact, it has given rise to a very important question and concern. That is, whether the next generation of Canadian men and women will be the first to have a lower standard of living than their parents.
The Speech from the Throne proposed some important objectives for the nation. These goals could include cutting illiteracy rates in half, ensuring that 90 per cent of Canadians attain high school diplomas or the equivalent by age 25, doubling the number of post-secondary graduates in mathematics, the sciences and engineering, and quadrupling the training provided by employers to their employees.
One member from the back says: Mind your own business.
I want to tell you: This is my business.

If you are here today, it is because one morning you woke up and found out that you were born and you were a Canadian.
It is because you are a Canadian that you turned out to be educated, so prosperous looking and so dignified from time to time.
These are valid and urgent objectives for a nation whose domestic lifeblood is international trade. Only substantial productivity improvements will restore and

sustain our competitive position and under-write our economic security.
The Speech from the Throne emphasized the need for Canadians to share in the benefit of prosperity and nowhere is this more true than in the case of aboriginal Canadians.
I have been gratified by the favourable response to the appointment of former Chief Justice Brian Dickson to advise the government on the membership and terms of reference of the Royal Commission on Aboriginal Affairs.
A few weeks ago in Victoria, I set out some of the progress now being made. First, the fast-track process is introduced to deal with land claims of $500,000 or less. Second, in order to accelerate claims processing, the authority of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to approve settlement payments without reference to the Treasury Board will be increased from $1 million to $7 million.
Third, some $355 million will be dedicated to this initiative over the next five years. This represents a quadrupling of resources for this program.
Fourth, the process will be made fairer by the establishment of a specific land claim commission.
Fifth, in co-operation with Indian leadership over the next few months, a joint Indian government working group will be established to address unresolved specific land claims process and public policy issues.
Finally, pre-Confederation land claims will be accepted for consideration for the first time.
Another native agenda initiative designed to help Indian leaders build a better future for their people is the Pathways To Success program. The objective of this program is to create a skilled, competitive aboriginal workforce. We anticipate investing approximately $200 million per year in aboriginal labour market programs.
As part of the native agenda we have increased the budget of the Indian post-secondary program by $320 million for a total expenditure of more than a billion dollars over five years. This year government assistance is making it possible for 22,000 Indians to go to college and to change their lives. When the member for Saint-Denis and I were going to college, there were fewer than
The Address
a hundred aboriginal students. This shows that some slow but steady progress is being achieved.
Perhaps the combination of the royal commission, strong support by Parliament and government, and constitutional change will provide our aboriginal peoples with the justice and the respect they have long deserved but have too frequently been denied.
Recently, the former Secretary General of the Commonwealth, Sonny Ramphal, said: "Canada is a model of stability in a multicultural world, and the breakup of the country would be seen as an encouragement for other societies to fly apart. Canada", he said, "has been something of a flagship of stability in a world of multicul-turalism; the Canadian model has been replicated around the world."

A handful of professional pessimists keeps focusing on the flaws in our political system. Of course there are flaws. No one ever said Canada or federalism were perfect. There are flaws, but the same professional pessimists who concentrate on those flaws and are always trying to obscure the greatness and strength of Canada, would have us succumb to their siren song and thus undermine our belief in the unity and greatness of this country. In Quebec, they are promising people the moon, and referring to economic and political unions that are purely imaginary. There are others outside Quebec who would have us believe that the best way to deal with the pervasive malaise in this country would be to separate Quebec from Canada.

Both sides of this pessimistic equation-those who want Quebec to leave Canada and those who insist that division is inevitable-both of these graduates, with doctorates in the school of pessimism, are completely wrong and they will be repudiated by history.

People who think Canada is a set of building blocks that can be rearranged at will or who think Canada can function just as well without one of its basic components are badly mistaken.

May 15, 1991
The Address

To strengthen our economic union, the federal government must exercise key economic powers and both levels of government must work together to secure our prosperity.
I believe it is possible in areas of federal jurisdiction to integrate explicit and effective inputs from regions and from citizens into the making of laws and policies. We must also find new and imaginative mechanisms to manage the interdependence of the federal and the provincial governments.
A look at the attribution of powers in 1867 provides a guide to the genuine thinking of the Fathers of Confederation when they created this country.
You will see that the erosion of many of those powers over the years has brought about quite a different country from that which they contemplated. This explains some of the serious problems that provinces feel, particularly as they are further and further removed from the centre, as they are more and more concerned about their capacity to protect language and culture and regional interests.
And so we must find new ways to manage the interdependence of the federal and provincial governments. Federalism is a balance between the need for central authority and the scope for decentralization to meet local aspirations. Its genius lies not in its perfection, because no system of government yet devised is perfect, but its genius comes from the fact that it combines self-rule and shared rule, sovereignty and association.
The challenge we face is to rebalance our federation, not to throw it out. This will be the most important challenge that we have to meet during this session. The eyes of the nation are turned toward this Chamber and all of its members. It is not the time to exacerbate our differences; I think, Mr. Speaker, it is the time to extol our diversity. This is not the time to weaken our country; it is the time to strengthen our resolve. It is not the time to point fingers; it is the time to join hands. This is not the time to turn our backs on the common destiny; it is the time to prepare a better country for all of our children.
On July 1, thousands of Canadians, young and old, French speaking and English speaking and first Canadians and recent immigrants, will stand outside this building and look to the top of the Peace Tower. They will see there the maple leaf, be witness to our history and the emblem of our future greatness. Indeed, my friend says "a great flag", and he is 100 per cent right.
Our challenge is to reject the call to selfishness and division and to point the way to a better Canada, a Canada that is more open and fair, and generous and free, which will become the pride of its citizens and a model for the entire world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to comment on the government's Speech from the Throne as well as on the Prime Minister's remarks just preceding this.
We have heard many members of this government say that this session could be the most important one since Confederation and I and my party certainly agree with that. We have also heard the government say that imagination will be required to move forward and emerge stronger from this crisis in which our nation finds itself. Again, we in the New Democratic Party agree with that. I have heard from this government that we are at a turning point in our history and once again, we agree.
In listening to the Speech from the Throne, what is most striking and most disturbing is that there is nothing in it to meet the challenges confronting Canada now. It contains the same old responses, the same failed eco-

nomic policies and the same flawed constitutional process.
It is saddening that this government has chosen and is determined to follow the same old course, because being at a turning point means turning. The government refuses to turn. Instead it goes blindly ahead and takes Canada into another dead-end. We must turn to find new directions and new ways, to find a destination and a new future for Canadians. That is the responsibility for all of us.
The throne speech identifies unity, competitiveness and responsive national government as priorities. Indeed, they should be because in the six years since this government took power, Canada has moved to a large degree from unity to disunity, from being globally competitive toward being globally uncompetitive, and from having functional national institutions to national institutions such as VIA Rail and the CBC that are mere skeletons of what they were when this government took power.
These are issues which must be addressed and I will do that today, but in a very different way than this government. I propose that we follow a people's agenda, an agenda that serves Canadians and Canadian families.
It is clear to everyone, except a few across from us in this House, that the Conservative corporate agenda has failed Canadians. I want to ensure the Canadian people that our party will not stand by and watch these six years be followed by another six years of this kind of failed economic planning.
This Parliament is charged with one responsibility this session. That responsibility is to work to build the kind of Canada that all Canadians want to belong to.

It means drafting a Constitution that will unite this country. It also means creating an economic, social and environmental partnership among Canadians and between governments and the people they represent.
Canada as we know it today is a country where 1.5 million people are jobless, where the gap between the rich and the poor is widening by the day and where the middle class is in the process of disappearing.
Our health system is in jeopardy, our education system is deteriorating and major social programs are being
The Address
eliminated. Moreover, the crucial environmental challenges we are facing are left unanswered. Every day sees another institution, a symbol of our Canadian identity, such as VIA Rail, Air Canada or the CBC, undermined or simply eradicated. The links that bond this country together are being cut unscrupulously. The problem is that the Prime Minister make a lot of fuss about the need to save Canada, but then his Minister of Finance tables a Budget that strikes at the heart and soul of this country. It will take more than declarations of love for Canada to save this nation and allow it to grow. It will take a government capable of making concrete commitments toward giving the country a strong and fair economy and strenghtening our social programs and national institutions. We will need a government committed to shaping Canada to be a better place to live for all Canadian men and women.
It would not be fair of me if, based on no evidence, I accused the government of a gap between its rhetoric and its action, so I draw your attention to the last throne speech delivered in 1989. It said that one of the government's objectives was:
-to maintain a caring, compassionate society which will be able, through continuing economic prosperity, to meet its obligations and responsibilities to those who are less fortunate and in greatest need.
What did the government do toward this end? It introduced the clawback to old age pensions and family allowances. It abandoned funding of unemployment insurance. It announced the delay of long-promised national child care programs. It introduced the GST. It capped funding for social programs to B.C., Alberta and Ontario. It froze transfer payments for post-secondary education and health care.
I have not read the most recent edition of the Oxford Dictionary, but it seems to me that unless the meanings of caring and compassionate have changed-the words that this government in 1989 said it cared about, that it wanted to make sure existed in Canada-they have been revised by what this government has done. The policies I have just cited which have been put forward by this government have nothing to do with caring and compassion, but everything to do with indifference to the ordinary Canadian.

The Address
Surely if we are to have a renewed Canada, we must build a nation in which all people can share in its bounty, in which all Canadians can participate and in which all Canadians feel they genuinely belong.
In this throne speech, the government speaks of the need to build an economy competitive globally. Global competitiveness is the new corporate catch phrase and I am sure we are going to hear a lot about it in the months and years ahead. The question is not whether we should be competitive, of course we should be. The question is how do we get there.
The government and the corporate community insist that there is only one road. That is to further cut workers' wages, to reduce benefits, to cut social programs, to provide fewer government services, to weaken government and diminish standards to the levels of countries such as Mexico.
There is another way. There is not just one way to become competitive. There is another way and that is by investing in people. It means investing in research and development, investing in training and education. It means strengthening programs which increase economic security, ability and productivity of workers to compete with high wage, high productivity and low unemployment countries such as Germany.
The choice is clear. We can reduce Canada to the lowest common standard or work to join the world's best. We, on this side, say let us work to join the world's best.

The hon. member for Mississauga South who will chair the Fiannce Committee stated recently that the Canadian worker, and I quote, "can either work harder for a lesser pay or not work at all. It is quite simple. That is what competitiveness is all about."
That may be how this government defines competitiveness but, for the record, the New Democratic Party will not let the govemement use this argument as a pretext to close down plants, to drive farmers to the brink of banckruptcy and to trample the rights of the Canadian workers' families.
The government must recognize that it is unacceptable that, for the sake of competitiveness, we have 1.5 million jobless people in our economy.
That is totally unjustifiable, Mr. Speaker. The NDP finds unacceptable as to the Canadian people.
The government undertook in the Speech from the Throne to create 2.5 million jobs by the year 2000. The question is how can that be done. That the government did not say.
I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, that this vague commitment will bring little comfort to the 10 percent plus Canadians who are without a jobs in 1991. It will not reassure the Canadian men and women who will loose their jobs in 1992, 1993, 1994 and so on, because this government has its mind set on pursuing destructive policies such as free trade, the GST, and high interest rates combined with an overvalued Canadian dollar.

While the 2.5 million job creation figure may sound impressive on the face of it, the reality is, given the fact that more people will be entering the workforce this decade and given the growth in the size of the workforce, the creation of 2.5 million jobs between now and the year 2000 will mean an unemployment rate, not of 4 per cent, not of 5 per cent, but of 10 per cent in the year 2000.

speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
This government is planning for permanent unemployment. A 10 per cent unemployment rate in Canada-millions of Canadians out of work-is not the New Democratic Party's definition of competitiveness. It clearly is the Conservative Party's definition of competitiveness: some workers have to be out of work; some workers cannot work; and some workers cannot be productive because that is going to be in the interests of this nation.
We say that is not in the interest of this nation. The human deficit is the largest deficit we have in Canada today.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The Prime Minister will say: "Well, we have created a lot of jobs". There is also the question of what kinds of jobs are being created.
A few days ago the finance minister said that to him, a job is a job is a job. There is little one can do in the face of such an insensitive remark but to ask the minister if he believes that a single mother forced to take a part-time job, making $100 a week, has a job just like a cabinet
May 15, 1991

The Address
minister who makes thousands of dollars a week or a lawyer or a corporate executive who makes over hundreds of dollars an hour.
What would he say to the women some of my colleagues spoke to yesterday, one of whom has a husband who is a trucker and has not had work for eight months, thanks to the policies of this government? Here is a woman who supports her family by making $300 a week, working six days a week, paying $625 a month in rent and who has not been able to buy her teenage daughter anything new in two years. Would that minister tell that woman that a job is a job is job? Well it is not. It is poverty.
Job creation is about more than poverty wage jobs. It is about creating full-time jobs that have decent wages and dignity. It is about pay and employment equity. It is about ensuring that child care is available for all Canadians who require it in order to make a living.
Job creation is also a matter of improving training, research and development and education. This is the front that this government has failed miserably on. It promised the trade adjustment program after the trade deal. For most Canadians, it never happened. Its cuts to the National Research Council have devastated that council, and that respected institution and this government's spending on R and D continue to lag behind those of our international competitors.
In the education field, after years of cutting transfer payments to the provinces for post-secondary education, with cuts of $3.8 billion between 1990 and 1995 alone, for this government to turn around and identify education as a primary national objective in the throne speech is the ultimate hypocrisy.
You cannot cut post-secondary funding just a mere three months ago and now identify education as a priority. Somehow, the government's actions have to match its words. Strong curriculum and teaching objectives and goals are all part of quality education but adequate funding is crucial. I would suggest that if this government is serious about education and about attacking the problem of illiteracy, it restore funding immediately.

One last comment on the economy, Mr. Speaker. It is interesting to note that the Speech from the Throne finally recognizes-better late than never-that economy and national unity are closely intertwined. I have been saying so for a long time.
To the Saskatchewan family facing the loss of its farm because of excessively high interest rates, interest rates are a matter of national unity. To the Windsor worker who has lost his job because of free trade, free trade is a matter of national unity.
To the young woman laid off by a textile industry in Montreal, it is also a matter of national unity. To the northern residents who must pay the GST when everything already costs so much, taxes are a matter of national unity.
Thus, for the sake of national unity and competitiveness, I ask the government to recognize once and for all that free trade, GST and high interest rates are bad policies that must be rescinded.

I would now like to comment on some of the other aspects of national unity in the agenda put forward by this government.
I would like to address in particular issues concerning the constitutional aspects of national unity and the call for non-partisan co-operation. There is absolutely no doubt in my mind that the future of Canada is more important than the fate of any one political party. It is more important than the career of any one of us in the House of Commons. Our decisions and actions in the coming months must be guided by that reality. The good of the nation comes first always.
I believe that we can find a way to work together for the good of the nation. I say to this House with honesty and with a depth of emotion that the members of the New Democratic Party will do all that we can to work to forge a common future. That is our responsibility and we take it very seriously.
At the same time, I say with honesty and emotion that the members of the New Democratic Party and all Canadians cannot be handed a take it or leave it deal and be told to accept it in the name of non-partisanship. Non-partisanship is about bringing people together into the process from the beginning. It is about truly listening,

May 15, 1991
The Address
incorporating constructive suggestions put forward and it is about respect. It is about respecting the views of others and it is about true co-operation. Non-partisanship does not mean playing by only one set of rules, the government's rules; it means setting the rules together.
I say to the government and to the Prime Minister: Let us begin by opening up the process. The establishment of another traditional parliamentary committee I think will signal to most Canadians more of the same, more of the old way, more of politicians talking to other politicians and more delays in dealing with the real issues.
This House could move to immediately establish a constituent assembly based on Canadian reality and on Canadian needs. There are many other models across the country, but we do not have to just accept those. We have enough innovation here. We could create our own, one that meets our own needs. We should establish that format so that Canadians are directly involved in the process from the beginning.
If we cannot start with something new, how will Canadians have any confidence that the result will be a new and renewed Canada?
I believe that we could have a constituent assembly where there would be elected officials and non-elected officials, where there would be a genuine guaranteed participation of aboriginal groups, women, northerners, multicultural and official language group communities in addition to participation by our elected colleagues in territorial and provincial legislatures.
I know the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs and the Prime Minister will say that a parliamentary committee, the traditional way as opposed to a constituent assembly, has been established by this government because it is up to elected representatives to take responsibility to set the course of the nation. By doing so, they will say, elected representatives will gain credibility and the trust of Canadians.
We elected representatives do have a crucial role but surely the way to earn the trust and support of Canadians is to demonstrate that we have been listening to what Canadians have been saying. Canadians have been saying: "We want a different way. We want to feel included in the process from the beginning".
It surely cannot be that difficult to be somewhat creative, somewhat innovative and to try something new
that will respond to the calls from the public and will be a truly co-operative effort in forging this new nation.
As it stands under the government's proposals now, which I hope it is prepared to reconsider, with the various committees that have been travelling the country and will travel the country, in the final analysis it will be the government itself that will be able to retain all levers of control, to decide what evidence it will hear and what it will listen to. Will it just perhaps follow an agenda that it intended to follow all along? That is something that we all as parliamentarians have to address; we are saying to Canadians at the beginning that their views count. I suggest we can do that by a process of including a broader range of people right from the beginning.
We must continue to work for a fair and open process because Canada quite simply cannot withstand another failed round of constitutional discussions.

As for the content of those discussions on national unity, my party will continue to put forward ideas that we sincerely believe will contribute to strenghtening our national unity.
We have already made positive suggestions on the contents of a new Constitution and on the need to not only conclude a constitutional agreement but also agreements on economy, environment and social programs.
Therefore, I ask the government and the Prime Minister, in the spirit of the call to non-partisanship that is reflected in the Speech from the Throne, to consider those propositions and try to integrate them into a program to strenghten national unity.
Let me close by saying that having recently travelled extensively throughout the country, I have seen a positive change in the mood of the country. I think some of the acrimony or the bitterness that emerged after the Meech Lake process has diminished, and Canadians are really beginning to renew their search for compromise and agreement.
I am optimistic that we can succeed in meeting the many issues before us, in meeting the unique responsibilities of Quebec, the home of French language and culture in North America, and in addressing the real concerns of aboriginal people, the west, Ontario, the
May 15, 1991

north, the Atlantic provinces and all the people who live within our borders.
I believe we can, through acknowledging diversity, make that diversity our true strength, our true uniqueness as a country. The goal must not simply be keeping Canada together; the goal must be building a truly better Canada.

speechtext:
There will in the coming months be much discussion about what is wrong with Canada, but let us never lose sight about what is right with Canada. Ours is really a marvellous achievement, an achievement of diverse cultures coming together, of people separated by great distances creating common bonds, and of individuals and communities sharing common values and common objectives.
I recently read something that a Canadian song writer, Andrew Cash, wrote when he returned from a trip to India, an old country that has a long history. He observed that Canada:
- has more space and time than, perhaps, any other nation in the world to be thoughtful and innovative, not just in accumulating wealth, but in the field of human understanding, in pioneering new ways for different peoples to live together in harmony.
It is our responsibility as parliamentarians to take this session of Parliament and use it to be thoughtful and innovative, to find new ways for Canadians to live together, to work with all Canadians in building a Canada that says to the world: "This is what can be achieved when a nation takes the gifts it has been given and dedicates itself to creating a society that values and cares about each and every one of us".
The New Democratic Party pledges to the Canadian people to work toward and offer constructive suggestions to make sure that this great country of Canada, the one that many of us grew up in, will be here for our children. In my view, we do not have the privilege of dealing away this country. We must take the responsibility for building it. I look forward to that task, as does my party, with great enthusiasm.

Mr. Speaker, a few moments ago we heard the Prime Minister calling
The Address
Canadians to take heed to the celebration that we will experience here on Parliament Hill on July 1.
The Prime Minister did not talk about the thousands upon thousands of Canadians who this July 1, like this June 1, like this May 1, will be experiencing hunger and frustration and disappointment and despair because this government is not meeting its responsibilities to Canadians.
I listened to the Prime Minister remind us of the fact that this is a country that must operate in the public interest. I could not agree more.
I have watched this government for six and a half years. This has been a government of the private interest. The private interest of American Express. When it wants to deal, there is a turn around time of 24 hours. The private interest of the Iraqi spokesperson. Thousands upon thousands of people around the world are waiting in line for months and years to come to Canada, but he receives a quick turnaround because he has a private interest.
The private interest of the Boeing Corporation. We remember when the Prime Minister, a mere two years ago, stood in the House and said that he was introducing legislation to save those jobs. Now the single largest employer in the city of Toronto has its livelihood threatened by a takeover from a company that is asking for $500 million in taxpayers' aid before it even guarantees Canadians jobs.
What is the public response of this government? Since the Tory takeover in 1984 of over 900 foreign takeovers, Investment Canada has not overturned a single takeover.
When the Prime Minister talks about the private interest and asks us to rally around the public interest of Canadians, I say to the Prime Minister there is a public interest here. There is the public interest of the women in the gallery today who were in tears. The members opposite may laugh and chuckle but those women were in tears because they saw their families' livelihood being dealt away by a trade deal signed by this Prime Minister.
In my own community there is the public interest of the steel workers. From December 1989 to December 1990, imports of steel from the United States, during this

May 15, 1991
The Address
great window of opportunity supposedly created by the trade deal, increased by 166 per cent while exports from Canada to the United States decreased by 12 per cent. Is it any wonder that in my own community over the last year unemployment has increased by 67 per cent?
I want to say to the Prime Minister that when he tells Canadians to wave the flag on Parliament Hill on July 1, he should also tell Canadians that by restoring the economy, the sound economy of this country, we will begin the road toward constitutional and economic sanity.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has made a fine speech today in the House and I would like to believe him. He has mentionned the fact that we must work together, that we should not indulge in narrow partisanship about the constitutional issues. I feel the same way and I completely agree with this idea, Mr. Speaker.
But we must remember, Mr. Speaker, who has indulged in partisanship for the last three years concerning the future of our country. It is the same man on the other side who claims now he is going to revitalize Canada, the very person who has created a situation where people, across the country, do not believe in our Canada.
It is neither the leader of the Opposition, nor I, the member for Hamilton East, it is not the other hon. members who have gone to Quebec, time and again, to tell them: "If the Lake Meech Acord is not ratified, you will be humiliated." It is the Prime Minister who has kept spreading this rumour. That is what he is doing, Mr. Speaker.
A wave of the magic wand and the Prime Minister is supposed to be able to restore a sense of team work here in the House of Commons. I want to believe him because I agree with the statement made by the House leader of the government side that this is probably a turning point in Canadian history.
Those Canadians outside the province of Quebec who see the constitutional question as just another chapter of Canadian sabre rattling are wrong. Those outside the province of Quebec who think they can merely excise the wishes-

-the will, the aspiration and the history of a people who has been living here for 400 years, I will tell them: You are wrong!

Those people outside the province of Quebec who believe, as does the leader of the new Reform Party, that you can have a Canada without Quebec are wrong.
There are two parties now on the federal scene who aspire to achieve political success at the expense of the country. On the one hand you have the bloc-

-who wants a Quebec without Canada. On the other hand, you have the Reform Party who wants to have a Canada without Quebec.

speechtext:
But in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, every hon. member, whatever his political colour or history who really wants to have a Canada, should understand de facto that it must include Quebec.

Those people in my own province who recently spoke before the Ontario committee on constitutional reform and believe that somehow the cost of separation would be borne only by a single province, their neighbouring province of Quebec, are wrong.
Thirty billion dollars worth of business takes place annually between my province and the province of Quebec. Those who think that we can arbitrarily cut them out of the Canadian equation at no cost to the rest of Canada are dead wrong.
The constitutional clock is ticking. On this side of the House we made very specific proposals. Last December we called for the Prime Minister to act immediately to give the parliamentary committee of Beaudoin-Edwards an expanded mandate. My leader, Jean Chretien, the only national leader to appear before the Belanger-Campeau committee, spoke in a very eloquent fashion about the steps that must be taken immediately to restore constitutional sanity to this country.
What have we had from the Prime Minister? We have had a disgusting exercise of constitutional strip-tease. He takes it off one by one by one. Two months ago he announced that he would be announcing an announce-
May 15, 1991

ment of an announcement next September of a committee that might have a chance to report sometime next year. Yesterday he announced the announcement of the committee of which the membership will be announced in September and we still do not know whether the committee will be mandated to examine a notion as simple as either a national referendum or a constituent assembly. Further chapters to follow.
I say to the Prime Minister, the time for the constitutional games are over. Now is the time to act, and to act in the best interest of all Canadians.

The Prime Minister told us earlier this afternoon- and I think everyone, including me, would agree with that, that the Parliament of Canada and our ability to survive as a nation is much more important than the fate of any political party, and that is true. Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I, as a Canadian, cannot help but ask myself a question, and I know that is tough. Some members close by will tell me: Mrs. Copps, you are being much too hard on the Prime Minister.
Mr. Speaker, do you think the Prime Minister can in fact regain the confidence of the people, after having lied so many times about the constitutional issue?
A few weeks ago, I held a public meeting in my constituency and about 300 people attended. I can tell you this was not an English community meeting, which does not even really exist, since 34 of the 35 people who took the floor chose not to speak in their mother tongue, English, and all of the participants, who wanted some answers about the economic situation, the interest rate policy, the monetary policy, and the constitutional policy, said: In order to rebuild this country, we have to get rid of the Prime Minister.

Mr. Speaker, we know the economic problems. We know the inflationary problems caused by this government's insidious GST. We also know that Canadians are unanimous on one question and it is that this Prime Minister has rolled the dice one too many times.
If this Prime Minister really cares about Canada, then maybe he should rethink his political future. Maybe he should step aside and give a chance to somebody who
The Address
really wants to rebuild this country. Maybe he should take the high road and let Canadians, by way of an election, choose for themselves the leader who can rebuild a true Canadian constitutional family. Take it to the people.
This Prime Minister expects all Canadians to rally around the absurd notion that he has taken the politics out of constitutional discussions. I sat here in the House when my leader was away on medical leave and watched the Prime Minister tear strips off him daily in his absence. I sat here as the self-same Prime Minister then called out to the opposition and said "we must be non-partisan".
We all realize how important this country is, and I for one was among those who were prepared to take a very difficult position on constitutional reform and support the Prime Minister, as I did in 1987. I believed that the capacity for reconciliation and the greater good of the country was more important than single political initiatives. But the Prime Minister has betrayed us too many times, and for him to come into the House today and ask Canadians to believe that he will be non-partisan on the issue of constitutional reform is just too difficult for Canadians to believe. It stretches the credulity of even the most silent backbencher on the government side.

Mr. Speaker, the next 14 months will be crucial in the history of Canada. I am not sure that the tide has turned yet, although the leader of the New Democratic Party said so in her remarks. But I think we have the ability to make the tide turn.
For example, we made very precise proposals in that regard. In fact, they included elements of Senate reform, elements of monetary policy reform, elements of power sharing reform, elements providing that all government levels would have to respond to the needs of every citizen and that any decision on power sharing would have to be made in the interests of the citizens, not of the government level.
When my leader attended the Belanger-Campeau Commission and when, after his appearance, he issued a statement in Montreal, he was very clear about the

May 15, 1991
The Address
timetable that we expected. Unfortunately, the government ignored it. I do not know why it is dragging its feet. Mr. Speaker, we already lost six months and we expect to lose another three. We lost almost a year before the Prime Minister gave Parliament the tools that are needed to reform the Constitution.
The Prime Minister argued earlier that the word of the people, the uppermost word, is the word of the Parliament. Why, then, does he not give us the tools, right now, so that we can start working to reestablish the constitutional sovereignty in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, we in the Liberal Party are prepared to start working now. We are prepared to start working today, because the constitutional clock is ticking and too much time has already been wasted.
We ask the Prime Minister, why wait until fall? Start now with the process of allowing the people of Canada to have their say through their elected members of Parliament. Unlike the NDP, we do not want to wait until Spicer and Beaudoin-Edwards report. Certainly their reports can be complementary to the work that is being done by this parliamentary committee, with the objective of looking at all aspects of constitutional change.
Given the time frames that are facing us, whether or not they are of our own choosing, they are a political reality. The time has come to get down to business in this Parliament.
It is strange, as we talk about the future of the country, as the Prime Minister himself says, so much is at stake. for constitutional reform to truly work, it has to involve the empowerment of every Canadian. It cannot be a special interest exercise.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with considerable pleasure that I rise today to comment on the speech of His Excellency the Governor General of Canada, which opened this session of the 34th Parliament.
His Excellency has expressed, on behalf of our government, a number of particularly pertinent themes. Our overriding concern at this time must be for the unity of our nation and, within that context, for all of the elements which contribute to a strong and vibrant Canada. This includes creating a political structure within which all Canadians can find free and full expression for their aspirations.
It also includes, as the throne speech rightly points out, the assurance of economic prosperity, of a clean environment, of improved representation and of a stable, compassionate and caring society.
If, as the throne speech states, the family is the most fundamental building block of Canadian society, then the elements of a strong and vibrant Canada must include the protection and nurturing of the family. It is for this reason that our government has committed itself to review its policies in relation to the family
This is a commitment that I and many of my colleagues have worked hard for and I want to express most sincerely my appreciation to the Prime Minister and his cabinet colleagues for listening to our concerns on this issue.
I am also grateful that this government has indicated that in the context of its over all plan for constitutional reform it is prepared to act to ensure that our support for families is effective, fair, efficient and above all, that the rights of families to choose their own lifestyles are protected. This commitment, I believe, is confirmed by the statement that "the test of constitutional reform will be fairness, effectiveness, efficiency and the protection afforded to the rights of all Canadians".
The family is the most fundamental building block of Canadian society. Strong families have had, and will continue to have, an enormous effect on building and strengthening our nation. No matter what part of the country we come from, we see this impact in our history.
We recall the early settlers of both our founding nations; the families of United Empire Loyalists who established themselves in the maritime provinces-

In Quebec, we know that families have been for a long time one of the pillars of the Quebecer society. Family respect and loyalty have played a key role in the building of the Quebec culture which is so rich, warm, distinct and open to the rest of Canada.

In Ontario and western Canada we celebrate the remembrance of our families, who often came in waves of immigration from England, Ireland, Germany, the Ukraine, from China and many other Asian countries, in fact from throughout the world. Everywhere in Canada our aboriginal peoples celebrate the endurance of their
May 15, 1991

families and often-times heroic endurance that has given them the strength to survive enormous cultural, social and economic change.
Whatever our origins, we all look back on our families and relate stories of how their courage and determination built our nation. It is only with strong families which feel secure in their inheritance that we can continue to grow and prosper as a nation.
I have to say that there are problems. Over the years our laws, particularly taxation laws, have not kept pace with the changes in society and in family structures. In our well-meaning attempts to fix problems we have created an extraordinarily complex system of deductions, credits, refundable credits, exemptions, support payments, sales tax credits and support programs; a system which almost no one can understand and one in which different elements often work at cross purposes or to the disadvantage of certain lifestyles, particularly traditional family lifestyles.
Although I will highlight certain examples today, I cannot refer to all of the anomalies in our laws and regulations which conspire against the family. Let me say, however, that I recognize that most of them are paradoxically rooted in the concept that the traditional family is the norm, and in old-fashioned and sometimes inappropriate concepts of dependency.
A simple example of this is the well-known case of two senior citizens each receiving the old age pension and the guaranteed income supplement. If they get married, they lose about $3,000 per year. Similar situations occur with veterans widows' allowances. If the survivor marries, the allowances are reduced or cut off. Examples abound in the Income Tax Act and I will come to these in more detail later.
The issue is that we constantly put an economic disincentive on marriage and that the government through its policies interferes in family decision making, particularly as it relates to child care.
Let us examine, then, the tax system as it affects families. I wish there was a way to make it simple but there is not, and that is part of the problem. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that you and my colleagues will bear with me.
The Address
The first issue is the impact of the tax system on marriage. Although the tax system is essentially based on individual income, rules have been introduced relating to certain credits where eligibility credits are based on family income. The GST is a good place to start. First let me say, without apology, that I support and supported this progressive and much-needed tax reform because I know that consumption taxes are fairer than income taxes which only penalize success. In my view, there is one important flaw in the GST. It relates to the credits for low income earners.
Because the rules refer to family income, the result is that two people living together, each making only $24,000 per year, that is with a family income of $48,000, can retain full GST credits and bonus credits totalling some $580. The minute they are married they lose the entire credit because their family income now exceeds the limit. In fact, two people making only $17,000 each would not be eligible for the credit if they were to marry. Add children to the family and the benefit to the unmarried couple is even more significant.
Another example is the principal residential exemption. Under the income tax system, profit from the sale of a home is considered non-taxable capital gains. This exempts the taxpayer from any capital gains tax on the sale of a home. Marrieds are permitted only one exemption because they are not permitted to share income. Since persons who just live together can share income, they are eligible for two exemptions.
There are also problems with the capital gains exemption, which I will not detail today because of the lack of time. However, they are similarly related to the examples just given.
What is also surprising is the rules for disabled attendant care. If an unmarried spouse is disabled, he or she can pay their spouse for care and claim a $5,000 deduction at income tax time if the disabled partner's tax rate is higher than that of his or her spouse. Again, marrieds are prevented from doing so by the attribution rules.
The equivalent to married exemption was intended to give single parents the same tax advantages that married couples enjoy, that is a spousal deduction. Unfortunately, many unmarried couples are manipulating the credit to their advantage. Unmarried couples with children can

The Address
claim two equivalent credits, each worth $1,400. As a result, the unmarried couple can be almost $1,300 better off after tax.
Let me give another example. The threshold of the refundable child tax credit is $24,800 and is based on family income. Unmarrieds can each make $24,000 and still receive their full credit. A married two-income family with the same incomes as the unmarried couple will lose the entire credit because their family income exceeds the threshold. In fact, the married family could have a family income of $17,000 less than the unmarried family income and still lose their entire credit.
The second major issue in the tax system is the combined effect of having only one earner in a family, along with the effect of marriage.
The first of these examples is the effect on family allowance. Family allowance rules require that the higher income spouse in a married family report the family allowance as income. Unmarried families can avoid this rule; the lower income spouse can claim the family allowance and reduce the tax burden of the higher income spouse.
The unmarried couple also benefits under the new family allowance repayment rules. Here family allowance benefits under this scheme are available in full only until the individual's income reaches $51,000. Unmarrieds can avoid the repayment threshold either through income splitting or by the lower income spouse claiming family allowance.
Two earner married families may not be able to use income splitting measures but they do benefit from the fact that the threshold is based on individual income. In a one-income family, the benefits are taxed back when the family's single earner's income is $51,000. A two-income family, however, with each parent earning $51,000, for a combined total of $102,000, retains their benefits in full. Concerning the child care deduction, if you are married you cannot pay your spouse to remain home and care for the children. If you are unmarried and living together with children, you can pay your spouse for caring for the children and then claim the payments for child care expense deduction which amount to $4,000 for each child under seven and $2,000 for children ages seven to fourteen.
Within the marriage category, however, the one income family is hit the hardest since it is only eligible for a $200 tax credit supplement to cover all the costs of raising children within the home. The working married couple on the other hand can obtain the full benefit of the deductions. The full costs of raising children within the home are not considered by the present system. The system interferes with parental decision making by making out of home child care the preferred economic option. The system is not neutral or passive.
To summarize the impact of just some of these rules, I would like to table an analysis of the tax circumstances of two families in Ontario. I have that here in both languages. In these examples each family has $60,000 of income. Similar examples could be presented from each of the provinces, but of course I am only presenting one here as an example.
One family lives a traditional life-style and has one income and three children, two under seven and one child over seven. One of the parents cares for the children at home. They are married. The other family is the same in every respect except that one of the younger children is unrelated to the others, both parents work-

speechtext:
The other family, as I was saying, is the same in every respect except that one of the younger children is unrelated to the others. Both parents work, earning $36,000 and $24,000, for a total of $60,000. The adults are not married.
Let me say at the outset that this analysis is designed to dramatize the impact of the Income Thx Act on these two families, but it does not by any means use all the loopholes that are available. It may seem incredible, but the total taxes paid by these two families differ by over $12,200. That is over $1,000 per month more tax that the traditional family pays. Almost half of this can be related to the $36,000-$24,000 income split. The other half is due only to the fact that the traditional couple is married.
May 15, 1991

In the examples that I have tabled, the income splitting effect has been separated from the marriage effect by also including data for a married couple with the same income split.
The tables show that the total taxes of a one earner family with three children and a family income of $60,000 are more than $6,700 higher than the two income married couple with the same number of children and the same income. The total taxes of a married two income couple with three children and a family income of $60,000 are more than $5,400 higher than the unmarried two earner couple in the same circumstances.
As I have said, the combined effect is that the total taxes of a one earner married couple with three children and a family income of $60,000 are more than $12,200 higher than for the unmarried couple in similar circumstances.
There is no doubt that we have a problem, but where do we go from here? The answer lies in the throne speech. We must carefully review not just tax legislation but all legislation that affects families. There is no easy solution. We are all aware of the difficult financial circumstances Canada faces with its mounting debt and seemingly intractable deficits. We need a complete review of all legislation and regulations that deal with family. Fairness must be the keystone of any response that we develop.
The other guiding principles in the throne speech-efficiency, effectiveness, and the protection of individual rights-must also be fundamental to our response. Directionally we must be certain that we are fiscally responsible. Family support already costs this government over $10 billion a year. Our challenge therefore is not to spend more money but to do a better job with what we have. The issue is fairness.
One of the difficulties we have is defining the family and developing laws that treat all families fairly. I submit that the definition of a family should not be based on relationships between adults, but on the presence and circumstances of children. Children define families and are its most vulnerable members.
Surely there are opportunities for us to combine the dizzying array of family support systems-family allowance, GST credits, child tax credits, equivalent to mar-
The Address
ried exemptions, spousal credits and social assistance plans, all of these-into one meaningful payment that can be directed to children based on their circumstances, not that of their parents. This would allow more meaningful support to be directed, for example, to children in single adult households who are truly disadvantaged. It would also mean that parents would have a greater freedom in deciding whether or not to care for their children at home.
An alternative would be to develop a system of family taxation, a system through which people gain access to preferred methods of taxation through commitment to family responsibilities.
Another approach might be to extend all family attribution rules to all persons in a household.
It is not my purpose today to propose an all encompassing solution to a very complex problem. Rather, it is to applaud our government and our Prime Minister for their forthrightness and courage in opening this subject up for discussion and for committing to review all aspects of government policy that relate to families.
An opportunity exists for us to re-establish the family as a unifying factor as we design our constitutional relationships. I can foresee a national program of family support that binds the country with common standards and commitments to national well-being, similar to our national medicare program and our pension legislation.
It may be appropriate to establish a program that is consistent nationally and can be augmented by provinces or regions to account for local differences in living standards, culture and lifestyles. This would mean abandoning the Canada Assistance Plan, but we must not be afraid to establish clearer responsibilities and delegate taxing authority to the specific level of government that has the spending responsibility.
Clearly, I support constitutional models which have some shared responsibilities, but which limit the national role to setting and taking responsibility for minimum national standards. I prefer universality and I hope that we can get away from complicated tax brackets.
In closing, we are faced with many problems, but also with an historic opportunity. In the context of revitalizing our Constitution, we can reassess our approach to families and develop laws which are, above all, fair to all families, which are effective and efficient, and which return to parents the primary responsibility and the

May 15, 1991
The Address
ability to choose what they consider the best form of upbringing for their children.
