speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I realize it is traditional to thank the mover and seconder of the Speech from the Throne at the outset of one's remarks. I will have the pleasure of doing that in a few moments.
I am still basically a broadcaster by instinct, and so I will lead my remarks with the news that today, May 15, within the past 24 hours, the man who was supposed to become the president of Yugoslavia, Stipe Mesic, was the man who told me that he would be the last president of Yugoslavia as we have known it.
When a parliamentary delegation, as part of the Canada/Europe Parliamentary Association met with Mr. Mesic three weeks ago, I asked the then Vice-President from Croatia: "Mr. Mesic, I ask this question with sadness, but will you be the last president of Yugoslavia?" He answered me directly: "Mr. Scott, you asked the question with sadness, I answer it with joy. Yes, I will be

the last president of Yugoslavia." Well, Stipe Mesic never got the chance to take over as head of one of the most politically turbulent countries in the civilized world, which I will point out in a few moments, makes Canada's troubles seem like a calm cul-de-sac with little butterflies, by comparison.
Not simply because of tradition, but also because of admiration for both gentlemen, may I sincerely congratulate the mover and the seconder of the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Saint-Maurice, and the hon. member for Regina-Wascana.
As you know, I have been around here covering Parliament in the news business, or sitting in this place as the member for Hamilton-Wentworth since 1958. During those 33 years, I have sat through dozens of throne speeches, and their movers and seconders, and I cannot remember in recent times when I have heard more eloquent testimony to the reasons this country should hang together than those presented by the former Mayor of Regina and my friend from Quebec, a fellow journalist by background. Well done, Larry. Their genuinely expressed feelings, from very different parts of Canada, about what it means to keep this country united, lead me directly to what the throne speech says about how we are viewed outside these borders.
Around the world Canada is respected for the constructive role we play in global affairs, for the protection we accord human rights. Millions of people around the world would gladly give up everything they have for the privilege in living in Canada.
Never did I realize that so profoundly as during a recent visit to Yugoslavia and Albania. I spent the Easter weekend in Albania, which is one of the most brutally repressed countries in eastern Europe as a result of 50 or 60 years of communism, as a result of an assignment by the Department of External Affairs. I also spent an unforgettable two days in Bulgaria while we were in eastern Europe. I will have more to say about those countries on another occasion. It is because there are so
The Address
many hundreds of thousands of Canadians of Yugoslav origin that I must weigh my next remarks carefully.
This 24 hours in Yugoslavia could be truly historic; today, May 15, could signal the end of Yugoslavia as we know and treasure it.
Let me quote the distinguished Toronto Star columnist, Richard Gwyn.
The country's present is defined by its past. North of a line essentially within Slovenia and Croatia you are still in central Europe. The towns and hamlets, neat and orderly, as if belonging to a poor province of Austria, and above all clearly European. South of the line, you are in the Balkans; everything is much poorer, is harder and starker and much more clearly Slav.
Mr. Gwyn points out:
While in London last week, the Croat president Franjo Tbdjman declared provocatively 'Serbs are another world and another civilization from Croats. It has long been probable that south Slavs, or Yugoslavs, would discover eventually that the common denominator was not enough to keep them together. Former President Tito did this by the power of his personality and by terror'.
To many Croats the creation of Yugoslavia was a forced partnership. The Croatian people never expressed a will to enter this state, according to one Croatian journalist. This two-way deep-seated mistrust has bubbled over as Croatia and Serbia clash over their differing views of a future Yugoslavia. The Serbian president Milosevic-and I will refer to him in a moment-and President Tbdjman "like to fight; they enjoy the hate", contends Milovan Djilas, a former communist dissident and long-time observer of the Yugoslav political scene.
Some analysts say the current crisis-the tanks, the armoured vehicles, the troops, the shootings, the deaths-has been used by the communist leader of Serbia, Slobodad Milosevic, to "step up demands for emergency measures" to stop Stipe Mesic from assuming the presidency of Yugoslavia today. Serbia is also determined to prevent Croatia from holding a planned referendum on independence this coming Sunday, May 19.
As of today, President Milosevic seems to have got his way. Mesic is a Croatian who is understandably vehemently opposed to the Serbian president and all his works. I guess that is why the Serbian president and others in the collective presidency ganged up on Mr. Mesic and denied him the natural right to the presidency.

May 15, 1991
The Address
Tourism is a $2.5 billion a year business for the country of Yugoslavia. It has been severely harmed by the last several months of unrest. Hardest hit have been towns along the Adriatic coast, like Makarska, which earn their livelihood from foreign visitors. The dispute in Yugoslavia sharpened several weeks ago when Croatian policemen were sent to protect Kijevo, a Croatian village inside the Serbian enclave. Serbs replied with a blockade of all traffic into the village, cutting off food and medical shipments.
Shortly after the Yugoslav army arrived to act as a buffer between the two sides. Croatians were incensed that the army, which is led by a predominantly Serbian officer corps, did not move to open up the road to Kijevo and they organized a demonstration against the military in Split, a coastal city with a major garrison.
That protest and others damaged Yugoslavia's reputation. Those pictures toured the world. As Yugoslavia reaches the front pages and the TV screens of the world media, I believe it would be foolhardy to think that we can contain the unrest and turmoil to the confines of southeastern Europe.
We are now watching the unravelling of an international state, the total collapse of the political and economic structure of Yugoslavia. Holding this country together, or as we discovered while travelling through the various republics, this country of countries, with apologies to my right hon. friend from Yellowhead, will be a dangerous game requiring great skill. Maybe the whole thing can be settled peacefully. Canadians of Yugoslav origin tell us that "a just divorce settlement can be reached after an unhappy marriage". Maybe, but do not count on it.
If anyone attempts by force to create a new state of states, the army will be called in, violence will be the continuing inevitable result and then equally inevitably, you will have a civil war. That episode would widen, I believe, into a much larger regional crisis extending far beyond the borders of Yugoslavia and would attract world-wide attention and concern.
I hope the Canadian government will urge the Secretary General of the United Nations to stand by and be ready to move quickly with UN mediation efforts in Yugoslavia if the situation deteriorates in the way I fear
it is doing now. The United Nations has been effective elsewhere around the world in containing those painfully difficult transitions on how to get from communism to democracy. That is really what this whole struggle in Yugoslavia is all about as tensions between the Serbians and the Croatians and the Muslims reach a fever pitch.
The Canadian delegation of parliamentarians to the various republics in Yugoslavia heard everyone talk about a peaceful resolution. We urged everyone to dissolve the union or restructure it, but do it peacefully. I can vividly remember the moment when I sat next to the President of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic. I literally erupted. I had my finger wagging, pleading with the communist boss of Serbia that we Canadians do not mind demonstrations. We tolerate and occasionally enjoy them in our country, including all the horn honking in front of the Parliament Buildings today. "But please, please for God sake", I asked the Serbian president, "try to avoid the international bloodstains of Yugoslavia's reputation by keeping your demonstrations peaceful as we try to do in Canada".
The official translator was simultaneously whispering in the president's ear. He kept nodding in apparent agreement. I am not sure what the enthusiastic handshake at the end of our encounter really meant, but I believe the violence one reads about on the front pages these days indicates that President Milosevic took my pleading with all the seriousness that he thought it deserved.
Yugoslavs are entirely on their own now. The west is no longer worried that the Soviets will try to exploit the situation now that the cold war is over. I am sad to say it, but I echo the words of Yugoslav's Mesic: "Croatia and Slovenia are just too European not to leave Yugoslavia sooner or later and enter Europe itself". I am deeply convinced after my travels through the many republics and the two provinces and after conversations with hundreds of Yugoslavs that some sort of loose federation is the only answer to the survival of the country as we know it. Were it not for the comments of somebody like Mesic, as I mentioned at the outset, I would optimistic that the collective presidency of the country might somehow result in a decision for the continuation of the multiplicity of states within a state. That collective presidency is meeting as I speak at this moment.

Even as a perennial optimist, I am doubtful about the outcome of this Sunday's referendum in Croatia and the resulting fallout. Now, as the crisis deepens, I think it is going to mean that Yugoslavians are going to have to keep stiff upper lips and white-knuckle their way through this, with hopefully a dash of diplomacy thrown in. Otherwise Yugoslavia may be just hours away from a full-fledged civil war.
Indeed, Slovenia has already been heading outward toward western Europe. Slovenia's local parliament has passed laws of dissociation from Yugoslavia. Does that sound familiar? Outright independence in Slovenia is planned for June. Croatia would like to do the same except for one slight problem. Of its five million people
600,000	are Serbs. Again, does that sound familiar? Quebec has 5,300,000 population, the English speaking minority, 637,000.
The tragedy of Yugoslavia sends a very real message to Canada. It is hard to believe that even the most nationalistic Quebecers cannot understand the consequences of dissociation, or separating. Quite simply it means the disintegration of Canada as we know it. Just as we are seeing the disintegration of Yugoslavia as we know it now, I thank God for the thrust in the throne speech which says, in effect, let us build Canada as we know it but let us build it better. I do not want to see my country break apart the way we are watching it happen right now in Yugoslavia.
The other welcome direction in the Speech from the Throne is the fact that individual members of Parliament will be allowed freedom from discipline by the government in order to give expression to our views and the views of our constituents. I am taking the government at its word so here goes.
I want the goods and services tax, the GST, removed immediately from feminine hygiene products. This government is taxing the menstrual cycle while exempting donated male sperm and sperm banks from the GST.
Time after time, phone call after phone call, I have received the same answer from the Department of Finance: "Sorry, feminine hygiene products don't qualify under GST-exempt regulations. They cannot be zerorated like male sperm".
The Address
I want the Minister of Finance to give me logical reasons why not. So far, all finance officials have told me is that these products are not health/medical related. I believe they are.
While I have received the utmost co-operation from both finance department officials and spokespersons from the Minister responsible for the Status of Women, the hon. member for Capilano-Howe Sound, I am still waiting for answers that make sense. I am going to keep the questions going until I get those answers, and until we get the GST removed from feminine hygiene products.
If I have time I would also like to draw to the attention of the House the outrageous largess that this government is lavishing upon one of Canada's greatest and wealthiest superstars, Wayne Gretzky. Why on earth should the Canadian taxpayer be subsidizing a Calgary-based company, Kevin Sports Toys, to the tune of $1 million for the "Great One's" blessing on NHL insignia and colours, with royalties in the millions, to the disadvantage of one of my Dundas companies, M.A. Henry Ltd., which is trying to make it on its own without government money?
Since M.A. Henry stands to suffer as a result of Ottawa's $1 million to Kevin Toys of Calgary, will somebody please tell me why this is being done at all? Why is this government not playing on a level board hockey table top? Can't Wayne Gretzky make enough millions on the ice without dipping into our pockets?
Mr. Speaker, I hope to have the chance to put these and other questions as the days in this Parliament roll on. I thank you and hon. members for your attention.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it certainly is a privilege for me to take part in this debate on the throne speech. I appreciate the opportunity to put a few thoughts and concerns on the parliamentary record.
The hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth can certainly count on my support in his efforts to remove the GST from feminine hygiene products. I would also hope that the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth would support the efforts of many, many Canadians, millions of Canadians, to have the GST removed from reading materials. After all, we live in an age of increased awareness about the need for education. In the opinion of this side of the House, the GST is a barrier. It is a barrier to reading, a barrier to education. The sooner it is removed from reading materials the better.
As we discuss the throne speech that was delivered this week, it reminds me of some observations that we made some weeks ago when we were thinking about this particular event, the delivery of the throne speech. There were a lot of commentators in Canada saying that the throne speech was to be this government's renaissance, this government's renewal. This was the document that was going to signal to all Canadians that this government was going to turn a comer. It was going to stop some of its bad old ways and adopt some new ideas, some new plans to give Canadians some hope, to give Canadians some plans to get us out of the recession.
I have looked at and listened to the throne speech and I would have to say, humbly, that it is empty. It was nothing more than a lot of rhetoric. Nothing more than a lot of words.
After you listened to the throne speech, would you want Brian Mulroney as Prime Minister for four more years? I doubt that many Canadians would answer yes to

May 15, 1991
The Address
that question. Only a pretty devoted Tory could answer that question in the affirmative.
Let us just take the national unity issue, for example. Are we farther along on the road toward national unity than we were before Brian Mulroney became Prime Minister of Canada? Not on your life. This country is in a mess. There are few Canadians who can recall so much disunity, so much doubt about our future. It is because of a Prime Minister who acted like a fool and was thinking more about himself and about power than he was about his country.
There was a referendum in the province of Quebec in 1980 and federalism won. The Constitution was patriated shortly thereafter.
In fact, the Prime Minister supported Mr. Trudeau at the time. There was no suggestion from Brian Mulroney then that Quebecers were humiliated. That is the word that the Prime Minister has used, that Quebecers were humiliated by the patriation process. It certainly was not his notion then, but somehow it is now. He was the man who went from coast to coast to coast in this country saying that if Meech Lake is defeated it is a rejection of Quebecers, something that could not be further from the truth. Yet that is what the Prime Minister said.
Is it little wonder we have so much disunity in this country? Is it little wonder there is so much grave concern for the future of this country? It is because we have had a Prime Minister who, to use that cliche that has been used so many times, rolled the dice once too often.
I worry that he is the kind of man who is apt to do it again. He is a man who will put his own political interest ahead of that of Canadians, ahead of that of this country. That is deplorable.
We were hoping on this side of the House that there would be some kind of plan. I am still on the issue of national unity. We were hoping the throne speech would contain some kind of plan to deal with the national unity problem head on. What did we get? Just more promises of talk, more promises of studies, more promises of commissions. That is not what this country needs now. This country needs leadership, firm leadership because we are in perilous times.
We cannot just fool around, dither, stall and wait until next fall for some kind of government plan. The clock is moving and we should not be waiting around.
On the issue of national unity, would we want the Prime Minister for another four years? The answer is a clear no.
Let us look at the issue of the economy. Remember how the Conservatives offered so much hope? We went through the recession in the early eighties. Not only did we have a recession, but the debt piled up. We had a deficit and the Tories came along and said: "There will be a Renaissance. There will be a renewal of the economy. Elect us and just watch us. See how we turn the economy around". A lot of Canadians bought into that. They elected the Conservatives. They elected Brian Mulroney.
Now it is almost seven years later and the economic despair that Canadians feel rivals the despair that was felt by our parents and our grandparents back in the so-called dirty thirties. Look at the figures: 1.5 million Canadians unemployed. Those are depression figures. Just in the last little while 19,000 Canadians have lost their assets through bankruptcy. Children are going hungry in this country, children are going to bed hungry every night.
Yet it was this government who said: "Give us a chance and we will revive the economy". They talked about the deficit and they talked about the debt.
We all know that the debt has doubled since 1984. People wonder where the the government spends all the money.
They increase taxes, they increase the debt 100 per cent, and they ask: what do they get for it? What do they see? How they howl about the deficit. How they bemoan the deficit. Very little happens, very little happens. It is a conundrum. It certainly is a conundrum for almost all Canadians, a government that says that a deficit is so pernicious to the economy that it really blocks our hopes and dreams for a better Canada, and yet it just sits there. It does very little about it.
It makes you wonder and it certainly makes you cynical. I have come to believe that this government would like to have the deficit there, perhaps forever, because it is the stick it uses to beat us over the head. It is the government's raison d'etre. Everything it does is all in the name of deficit reduction. It goes ahead and destroys our public institutions, our democratic institutions and

destroys Canadians' ability to have a better economy, all in the name of deficit reduction. We get the destruction, but we never get the deficit down. It makes you wonder, does it not?
God forbid if we ever had this government for another 10 or 20 years. My guess is that if it were here for another 10 or 20 years we would still have its deficit. It has absolutely no credibility whatsoever when it comes to deficit reduction, none, absolutely none.
Remember the former Minister of Finance, now the Minister for International Trade and some other things, and how we had to have high interest rates to beat down inflation, to wring inflation out of the economy? We have noticed in the past few weeks a reversal. Now we have to have lower interest rates. So what is it? Is it high interest rates that Michael Wilson espouses? Is that what he embraces? Or is it now lower interest rates?
There is the high dollar. The former finance minister, who preaches an economic philosophy that is supposed to be the be-all and end-all to our problems, creates a high dollar which is a barrier and an impediment to our exporters. How many business people in this country have asked for a lower dollar? How many business people have asked for lower interest rates? The government does not listen, except now in the last few weeks when there has apparently been this conversion on the part of the government, on the part of the former finance minister, and I suppose on the part of the current finance minister that we need lower interest rates.
I ask the question again: Would we really want the Prime Minister for another four years? The answer from this side is no. I notice that the good Minister of Justice would like to have him for another four years. I think she should reflect on that. I think it is a poor reflection of her judgment.
It seems to me that based on this throne speech this government is jaded, it is exhausted, it has no ideas, it is drifting and it is stalling. It is in stall and it has lost absolutely all moral authority to govern.
The Address
Canadians have said that in spades. They do not want this government around any more. Just look at the polls. They do not want this government any more. The sooner they can get rid of it, the happier they will be.
Medicare has been eroded by this government. It is the cornerstone of our social programs-my guess is that 95 to 99 per cent of Canadians support it-and yet there is no mention of medicare in the throne speech. In the last session of the House, we on this side put forward a motion asking the government to reaffirm its support of medicare. It said "no".
It voted against that motion. Now we find-given its negative vote on the motion, and it should not come as any great surprise-that there is no mention of medicare in the throne speech.
I come from western Canada. There is no mention of Senate reform. I think that the Prime Minister alluded to some kind of Senate reform. He was very vague in his remarks this afternoon but in the throne speech there was no suggestion of an elected Senate; none whatsoever.
Western Canadians are demanding a greater voice. They are demanding equality. That is what they want. They want a change in their parliamentary institutions. Western Canadians want an elected Senate right now. What do we get from this government? Zero.
Western Canadians will disapprove of any government that continues to bury its head in the sand.
I could not find the word "agriculture" in the throne speech, and yet down on the farm times have not been tougher.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pride that I rise today, and I thank the House for giving me this opportunity. I believe this Speech from the Throne was one of the most important this government has presented and I think that it meets the aspirations and expectations of the Canadian people as to what we want to become.
Mr. Speaker, I represent the marvelous riding of Argenteuil-Papineau, as you know. There are 55 municipalities within my riding, from Lac-des-Deux-Mon-tagnes, at one extremity, to Plaisance, in the Petite Nation area, at the other with Morin Heights and Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard to the north. Culture is febrile in my riding which I would describe as a microcosm of Quebec society and perhaps our Canadian society. Indeed, it is predominantly French-speaking, although a substantial English-speaking minority lives in the La-chute area, in the north and centre of the riding. As a matter of fact, those are people I come across regularly and they have been living in harmony with the francophone community forever.
Of course, it happens that we have some minor of problems communication, but friendship, or the neighborhood spirit as we say, makes for good relations. We too have our share of marginal elements who would like to sever our connections with the rest of Canada or to force the people of Quebec to take actions much more centered on one issue. As the . saying goes, it is not a matter of the head but of the heart. So, for my constituents, the whole constitutional issue is veiy much a matter of the heart.
I think they have been deeply hurt by the failure of Meech. That is what I hear when I tour the riding anyway. I consult my constituents as much as I can and let them know for instance when I have breakfast with some of them as I do sometimes-be it only for my personal satisfaction-that I would rather spend seven
May 15, 1991

days a week in my riding meeting and discussing with them, but that duty calls in Ottawa.
What I am told on such occasions, Mr. Speaker, is that they want respect. The French Canadians want us, their fellow citizens, to respect the fact that they are Frenchspeaking and want to live in harmony in the predominantly English-speaking North-American culture. I think that the English-speaking community in my riding misundertood, and certainly did not quite stomach-I have to mention this to give an accurate account of what they tell me, the Quebec sign law, Bill 178. They saw it as an attack on their personal and individual rights while, for their francophone counterparts, it was merely a collective expression of the will to preserve their culture and to save whatever little French fact was left in North America.
Mr. Speaker, the men and women in my riding are also telling me that there is, of course, a world of difference between what is told and what actually happens. The constitutional debates have always been emotionally charged. That is nothing new! Take the 1980 referendum for instance. Just this past Tuesday, Mr. Speaker, people I considered as ardent nationalists and separatists were telling me that, with the passing of time, they are not so sure anymore that Quebec should separate, that separating would be a good thing for Quebecers. They have come to realize that, finally, every effort should be made to save this great country of ours.
We often forget to remind ourselves that our country is the second largest in the world, with its border stretching over 8,850 kilometers. That is huge. There is a saying, Mr. Speaker, according to which one cannot appreciate what one does not know. Often, we think that the people of Manitoba and Alberta must be quite tough. But that is not true. When we travel there, we feel very welcome. Some of my constituents visited Western Canada and they were delighted, and even surprised, by the reception they got.
Mr. Speaker, whenever I travel throughout Canada, I know I will be warmly greeted by the vast majority of Canadians. Quebecers have always had a strong personality. They are very open. They try very hard to speak English when English-speaking tourists stop them for information or directions. Quebecers are a very generous people. Everyone I met either in Atlantic or Western
The Address
Canada have told me: There is a world of difference between what we hear and what really happen. Sometimes, we get a dangerously distorted picture simply because of some minor details.
Mr. Speaker, if I mention all this it is because I want to relate an incident which has affected my constituents very deeply. When a very small group of dissidents trampled the Quebec flag in the Sault Ste Marie area, I think it was, when-

The government machinery is indeed an administrative monster and I hope that in his Speech from the Throne the Prime Minister gave an inkling of great progress in that regard. That government machinery really has to be reformed, because the right hand in there does not know what the left hand is doing. The worst department, in my opinion, is the Revenue Department, the Taxation Department. It is totally absurd because they are dealing with the same taxpayer.
Mr. Speaker, some things also are absolutely incredible. Recently, in my riding, in spite of very harsh budget cuts, we managed to convince the Minister of Transport to grant the municipality of Lachute a small sum of $80,000 to repair the municipal airport located a few kilometres from Mirabel, whose future possibilities are outstanding. But, believe it or not, since it was money coming from the federal government, Quebec had to go through an enormous amount of red tape in order to

May 15, 1991

enable the municipality to spend this small amount of $80,000 on repairs needed at the airport.
So, the Economic Development Board, the municipality of Lachute, the Chamber of Commerce, all these bodies want to know what is the reason for these anomalies because everybody, including foreign investors, is waiting for these repairs and because it is only a study.
Certain things should not be, Mr. Speaker, and our constituents have reason to complain about government, at all levels. I only mention those two points because there would be too many, and I would need all my time if I were to mention them all.
Also, when I ask my constituents: "Listen, you say that we do not make enough cuts, that we must make more cuts. It is insane, the deficit is way too high. Where will that lead us?" And I tell them: "Give me some examples where we could make cuts."

There, I can tell you that our constituents are just like us. You know, governments really reflect society. We must also submit to soul-searching. We also find it difficult to decide where to cut. It is all very well to talk, but again when it is time to act, all is different. Where shall we cut?
It happens every time-let me digress a little-during the debate on GST, as a matter of fact, most of the business representatives, and I will give no percentages, came before the Committee on Finance studying the tax and said: "Yes, GST is excellent; it's a necessary evil, but you must apply it. Go ahead, there is no problem; tax on manufactured goods is not good for businesses, we agree. However, please exempt us for such or such a reason." So, at the end of the proceedings, we realized that most businesses wanted cuts, but not on them.
It's always the same situation, Mr. Speaker, everywhere. People are concerned with their daily activities, for you know that besides political ideologies, there is a daily life for our constituents and it is not easy. I witnessed plant closures in my riding and I can tell you that I was first to wonder if free trade was responsible for all that. Many of my constituents believed so. But, after
meeting with people and speaking to them, I came to the conclusion that most of those closures were due to mismanagement, overexpansion; those were businesses which used to manage growth but suddenly were unable to manage downsizing. In brief, they were unable to stand up to the challenge.
However, our constituents realize that we are living in an extremely generous society and that we are so spoiled that we consume frantically, Mr. Speaker, me included. I do not say that only for others, I include myself in the picture. So we consumed so much that we did not ask ourselves if it was harmful to the environment, if natural resources were there forever without creating any problem. Our quality of life demands that we own two cars and that we go to restaurants at least twice a week. Anyway, you know, we consume a lot and we work twice as much. Where is the quality of life for the families?
Tbday, we talk about latch key children, those who arrive from school before their mothers get home from work. Why? It is often because the family needs money, consumes a lot, needs a lot of money to face its commitments. Finally, who suffers? It is the latch key children.
Mr. Speaker, where is our quality of life now? That is the question that I ask myself. When women, more often than not-I know that, nowadays, men are greatly involved in the issue of child care-but we must say that it is often women who have to face child care problems. These women work inside the home and outside the home and are exhausted. How do you think families can cope with that without any problem?
Mr. Speaker, we always say that we have the governments that we deserve. But what can we do individually, each and everyone, in our own backyard? What can we do at home to set an example? We say: If things are bad, the government is to blame. But we do not want to look at our own faults. What do we do? Do we consume too much? No. Do you know what we do, Mr. Speaker? We put our garbage on the sidewalk and we say: I don't care where this is going, as long as it is not in my backyard. A truck comes around and goes away with our garbage. But then, when we talk about waste management, sanitary landfills, and so on, we say: "Take that anywhere, but not in my backyard!"
May 15, 1991

You see, we have a conscience. I believe we should, all of us, ask ourselves a question: "Where are we going, and what can we do individually to prove that we can, too, tighten our belt?" We ask the government to cut, but we should be in a position to tell the government where to cut. Are we capable today, when we want services, more services, of saying that we will pay for them?
Mr. Speaker, time is running out, and I still have so many things to add that I would need more than the 20 minutes allowed. I know that I still have some time left, and I would like to come back to the Speech from the Throne. The government said that it would act on the education level. For some persons, it may look as if the gouvemment will intervene in matters under provincial jurisdiction. At first sight, when we look at it cooly, rapidly, we may think that it could be true. But if we analyse it further, we have to look at the clientele it will serve in the long run. This is aimed at illiterate people, people who cannot read nor write, and who are desperate.
So, if we consider the people this is designed for, we will be less inclined to think that it is a question of provincial jurisdiction. Lets take the case of the Canada Health Act for exemple. We have national standards, but this issue falls under provincial jurisdiction. Why not have national standards in education for literacy and the like, while this issue would still fall under provincial jurisdiction? It is something that I would like to know. Like every Quebecer, I fiercely defend my province's juristictions and I would not like an important federal interference in these areas.
The government also mentioned the native issue. Mr. Speaker, my riding went through a crisis last summer. I talked about it in my speech after the Oka crisis. The members of this House should not worry. In my opinion, there will not be another crisis this summer. I do not think so, because the Oka people has once again realized that a very small group-let us not be afraid of stating the facts as they are-a very small group of armed warriors hiding behind masks came to Oka against the will of a majority of Kanesatake citizens. What did they do? Four or five persons managed to attract the national medias' attention and thereafter, everyone thought that all Mohawks were like that. Such a parallel bears
The Address
importance in relation to what I said about the Quebec flag.
So I must say no, Mr. Speaker, though the populations of Oka and Kanesatake have a hard time recovering from that serious crisis, they do not want another one, absolutely not, not even anything close to what happened last summer.
However, now that our eyes have thus been opened concerning the aboriginal question, my constituants and,
I think, every Canadian man and woman, wants to know what sovereignty means. They ask me: "Mrs. Bourgault, does that mean that the warriors, the Mohawks will continue to illegally sell cigarettes and deal in illicit gambling? Is that what sovereignty means? While a few miles away, in Oka, I sell cigarettes and that Indian is also selling cigarettes. Will sovereignty mean that he will be able to sell his cheaper than mine?" Those are basic questions that our constituents ask.
It is the same thing with the administration of justice and family matters, for example. I think all members must have felt a tremendous sadness last week when once again we saw a case of violence against women, a woman who was killed by an ex-inmate and who was kept three days in her apartment. We cannot remain unmoved when we hear about such cases, and with the Minister responsible for the Status of Women, I hope we will find solutions. I hope we will go beyond talking and actually find concrete solutions and see how Canadian men and women, how we as a community can stop, can wipe out this incredible and intolerable violence being inflicted on women and children.
Mr. Speaker, I am interested in fiscal justice. There is a group called the alliance for fiscal justice, which has proved beyond a doubt that the tax system is more favourable for couples living common law with children, than for married couples. This is unacceptable.
Mr. Speaker, I agree that we should change the way Ottawa works, as I said before, but the government and Canadian society must get together to analyse their needs and ensure that the government responds to the wishes of the citizens of this great federation, because, Mr. Speaker, my constituents tell me: It must be attractive. If you want us to stay in Canada-that is what Quebecers tell us-make it sound attractive. Prove that we can live and continue to prosper and be respected as francophones in Canada. If we do that, Mr. Speaker,

May 15, 1991
The Address
they will stay and give us one last chance. Thank you for your attention.

time members of the opposition should be allowed to vote with the government on other occasions.
I certainly agree with more freedom in Parliament. My hon. friend says we want to blame everybody else but ourselves. Fair enough, I agree with that; maybe we, as citizens of this great country, want to blame everybody else but ourselves. So maybe I am an elected member of Parliament representing constituents who are saying that "It is not my fault, it is your fault". We should think of stopping that sort of belief and bring forward some tough new proposals that will keep this country as economically viable as it should be.

Mr. Speaker, first, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Argenteuil- Papineau who certainly spoke from her heart in this House. However, I want to ask her a question about what she said with regard to Quebec because she is very interested in Quebec matters. She made me shiver when, speaking about education, she said she was concerned at first when she heard that the federal government wanted to get involved in education but that she felt reassured when she listened to the arguments put forward by others, and realized that it was a good thing for the illeterates, etc.
I can hardly believe that. She even referred to "national standards". I am convinced that the hon. member for Argenteuil-Papineau didn't come up herself with the idea that the federal government could set national standards in education. She knows that Maurice Duples-sis would be turning in his grave if there were such national standards.
So, I want to know what she really thinks. I know that she thought about that question. Yes or no, should the government of Canada infringe on Quebec exclusive jurisdiction over education?

What I meant when I referred to national standards in education-as they say, let's not get carried away, we have to look at this in the perspective of responding to a

May 15, 1991
The Address
serious national problem: the number of Canadian men and women who are illiterate.
Now, whether a more national standard is the answer-I am being very careful, so that my constituents and Quebecers generally won't think I agree with federal involvement in provincial jurisdictions-on the other hand, I am trying to consider the target population, in other words, people who cannot read. I think that with the help of the federal government and the provinces, we could deal with this matter by negotiating an agreement that would be for this particular group only.
So that is what I had in mind. However, all this is still up in the air. We don't know the details of the proposal mentioned in the Speech from the Throne. I would be delighted to discuss the matter with the hon. member as soon as we have more details.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate this evening in the time left allotted to me in the throne speech debate.
After having read the document, any Canadian who viewed the debate thus far or read the media could easily draw the conclusion that at the very least, the government was consistent with its record since 1984. It was consistent in the sense of unfulfilled expectations and broken promises.
It was only last week, before the House resumed, that the House leader on the government side said that this throne speech was going to be the most important throne speech in the history of the country, and therefore it was the government itself that elevated the expectations on behalf of Canadians, thinking there were going to be some remedies to the problems and difficulties embracing and afflicting Canadians from coast to coast.
As has been done time in and time out, the Canadian people and Canada have been let down. They had raised the stakes and all that Canadians have received through this throne speech is a document filled with very empty and general platitudes. Not only was it a heightened expectation, but somehow this was supposed to be the second track of how the government was going to usher in "the new agenda."
The first track was with a reshuffling of cabinet some days ago, a reshuffling of the same cards in the same deck. It was a case of the same old tired faces being reshuffled into new positions. If you were a business person and your executives had failed in their departments, I do not think there would be too many business owners today in Canada that would not only not remove those individuals, but in fact promote them.
The second prong of the new agenda was to be this throne speech, probably for the country and, politically speaking, for the Conservative Party. What we have in the pages of the throne speech read by His Excellency the Governor General, is simply a reflection of a very tired, a very insensitive and a very unimaginative government. Its fatigue is colossal, one that has crippled them into trying to crystallize Canadians' aspirations and dreams across the land.
How do we judge a throne speech? One way that the success of any throne speech delivered in this place ought to be measured is how Canadians, average Canadians, relate to this document. That is to say that we should not be engulfed in reading a throne speech for the purposes of members of Parliament, senators and the national media.
Somehow the throne speech has to have meaning to Canadians on the streets of Canada.
When a laid-off construction worker in York West looks at or hears about this document, what does it mean to that laid-off construction worker? What does this document mean to a plant that is either downsizing or about to be shut down on Toryork Avenue in my riding?
What does it mean to a university student who, after completing exams at the end of last month, graduates and is about to seek his or her place in Canada? Does it move a nation? Does it have a sense of purpose? Does it give definition or clarity to a direction of Canada? Does it serve to right the wrongs in the last number of years?
Does it say: "Maybe some policies we ushered in, perhaps with the best of intentions, has not worked? We are prepared to have the strength and the courage of a government to say so, to recognize it and to put something different in its place".
The throne speech does none of the above. The average Canadian who may or may not have a job cannot take solace from this throne speech. If the average
May 15, 1991

Canadian cannot identify with a throne speech, then why do we have the pomp and the ceremony? Why do we spend hours debating a document that 200 feet from Parliament means very little?
It is an abuse of our democratic institution if it has no meaning at the base of our country.
Talking about the aspirations of the average Canadian, one can quickly and very genetically summarize the two great challenges facing our country at this time, the issue of national unity, and the issue of the faltering economy and the recession in which Canadians find themselves.
On national unity, you pick up the throne speech and you search for the answers. There are not any. The response of the Prime Minister on behalf of his government on the question of national unity is delay.
What he proposes in the throne speech is the creation of another committee that will not be mandated until September. To make matters worse, that committee will be given a lifetime of another five months to report back to this Parliament and to this government.
It will not be until January or February of 1992 that the national Government of Canada will say anything definitive about our Constitution when, in fact, the Government of Quebec, to its own credit because it is taking care of its own house, is already making it very precise on when the potential dates of a referendum will be.
We have a national government, mandated to speak for the country of 26 million Canadians, which is unable to say anything definitively until February 1992. That is a shame and irresponsibility at its height.
If the fragile state of the nation was not as bad as it is, then perhaps a bit of time and consultations would have been legitimate and very much warranted.
Mr. Speaker, I ask you: In the midst of a national unity crisis of sorts, we will not hear anything from this government until February 1992. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that it is not because Canadians ought not to be consulted. I am very confident of what I am picking up among Canadians.
They are absolutely sick and tired of being studied to death by this government. Whether it is the issue of unity, whether it is the issue of economy or whether it is
The Address
the issue of trucking, this government simply hides behind the word "study".
On the question of national unity, we have had a number of committees and commissions, provincial and federal, travelling across the country. Canadians are saying to this government: "It is time for our country to be rallied. It is time for our country to be rallied to a point of strength and confidence, not to be rallied to a point of study, indifference and indecisiveness". That is not national leadership. That is only a manifestation of an absence of national leadership and national purpose.
This is the failure of the government. Let us make it perfectly and crystal clear. Let us not have Canadians lose hope in themselves and in their country because we have a team on the other side that cannot shoot straight. Let us not have the failures of the government be the failures of Canada.
That is why my leader, my caucus and my party decided to try to rally that confidence of Canadians. We put out a challenge to the government. We have initiated through a series of speeches across the country a nine point program, a vision of the country that we have asked the government to try to respond to, to try to kick-start a debate, to try to bring Canadians and wrap the strands together. My friends, unless Canadians are confident in themselves and of this country, we will be unable to come to grips with the challenges and the problems that confront us.
We did not wait for a committee to report. We did not wait to appoint our members on that committee. We did not wait for a white paper, a black paper, a yellow paper. My leader did what he does best. He spoke frankly on behalf of this country. He has also given the opportunity to Canadians to ratify through a national referendum.
Yes, a referendum can be divisive. My leader clearly was at the forefront of the last referendum in Quebec in 1980. However, this party also believes that if we are going to get a referendum in Quebec, then what is wrong with extending that opportunity to the other Canadians across the country? What is wrong with not giving a stake to the 26 million shareholders who equally own a piece of this country called Canada? There is nothing wrong

May 15, 1991
The Address
for those 26 million shareholders on a given day to mark their ballot on behalf of Canada.
Therefore, not only do we speak of a vision of this country, a program for constitutional reform, but we have not dithered or dallied: Do we have a referendum, do we have an election, do we have a constituency assembly? We have said: "Give those people, those shareholders, an opportunity at the end of the day to speak for themselves and for their country".
I challenge the Prime Minister and his government not to wait, not to study, not to fiddle while anger, jobs and national unity bum, but to act as they were elected to do. If the Conservatives are unable to act responsibly, if they are unable to provide the leadership, then they do not deserve the responsibility of sitting to the right of the Speaker. They should vacate and vacate quickly.
The other challenge is economic vitality. We have a recession made in Canada by Conservatives. We have the situation where there is a high dollar, high interest rates, plant closings across the country, jobs lost and lost permanently, jobs that will not come back. We have structural changes to make in the face of world change. What does this throne speech say of those realities facing Canadians? Absolutely nothing.
Once again I return to the premise of my argument. If this throne speech does not mean anything for that unemployed Canadians, then the throne speech has failed and failed miserably.
I see that you are signalling me, Mr. Speaker, and I look forward to continuing tomorrow.
